Secretary 

The Secretary is responsible for the administration of the functions and authorities assigned to the Department of Commerce by law and for advising the President on Federal policy and programs affecting the industrial and commercial segments of the national within the economy of the Department. scope 

ASSISTANT TO THE SECRETARY.- 

The Assistant to the Secretary is the principal staff assistant to the Secretary. He assists, advises, and acts on behalf of the Secretary on such matters of administration and policy as the Secretary directs.

SPECIAL ASSISTANT TO THE SECRE- TARY FOR PUBLIC AFFAIRS.-The Spe cial Assistant to the Secretary for 

Public Affairs advises the Secretary and other officers of the Department on public affairs matters. Through the 

Office of Public Information he guides and directs all informational programs within the Department. 

OFFICE OF CONGRESSIONAL RELA- TIONS. The Special Assistant to the Secretary for Congressional Relations advises the Secretary and other officers of the Department on congressional relations. This office provides information to the Congress on the programs of the Department and supervises the handling of congressional correspondence and inquiries. It keeps the Department advised of the progress of the Department's legislative program in the Congress and of other pertinent congressional activity. 

Under Secretary

The Under Secretary of Commerce serves as the principal deputy of the 

Secretary, performing continuing and special duties as the Secretary may assign from time to time. He exercises policy direction and general supervision over the United States Travel

Service. He also serves as acting Secretary in the Secretary's absence. 

Assistant Secretary for Economic

Affairs serves 

The Assistant Secretary for Economic Affairs as principal adviser to the Secretary on broad, longrange, economic programs, as well as adviser to other departmental officials with respect to matters of economic policy positions and recommendations.

His responsibilities include coordination and review of the economic research and statistical programs in the Department. He serves as the Department's liaison with the Council of Economic Advisers. He also exercises policy direction and general supervision over the Bureau of the Census and the 

Office of Business Economics. 

Assistant Secretary for Domestic and 

International Business 

The Assistant Secretary for Domestic and International Business serves as the principal adviser to the Secretary on all domestic and international aspects of the Department's responsibilities concerning industry, trade, investment, and related economic activities. He exercises policy direction over the Bureau of International Commerce, the Busi ness and Defense Services Administra tion, the Office of Field Services, and the Office of Foreign Commercial 

Services. 

Assistant Secretary for Science and

Technology 

The Assistant Secretary for Science and Technology serves as the principal adviser to the Secretary as well as adviser to all departmental officials with respect to matters of science and tech- HADVARN HAW (AR)

Assistant Secretary for Economic

The Assistant Secretary for Economic Development serves as the principal adviser to the Secretary on matters concerning the economic development of States, regions, areas, districts, centers, and communities in the United States, as well as adviser to other departmental officials with respect to such matters. OFFICE OF MANAGEMENT AND ORGA- NIZATION. This office advises on and conducts studies of organization structure and management problems, engages in activities to extend the proper use of computers as well as other management tools and techniques, and promotes management improvement efforts throughout the Department.

APPEALS BOARD.-The Appeals 

Board consists of a full-time chairman, appointed by the Secretary, and a number of departmental officials serving as Board members in addition to their regular duties. The Board decides disputes under contracts entered into by the several bureaus (other than the Maritime Administration) within the Department. It also considers appeals from the public in respect to certain administrative and regulatory actions under the Export Control, De fense Production, and Surplus Property Disposal Acts. 

Office of Administration (DIB) 

This office provides administrative management services to the organization units under the Assistant Secretary for Domestic and International Business. The Director of this office serves as the administrative officer for these organization units. This office also conducts studies and coordinates U.S.

Government participation in approved international expositions to be held in the United States.

SPECIAL ASSISTANT FOR EQUAL OP- PORTUNITY. This official develops policies and procedures for compliance throughout the Department with equal opportunity statutes and regulations, and provides staff assistance to the 

Assistant Secretary for Administration in the latter's Department-wide responsibilities on equal opportunity matters. 

The General Counsel The General Counsel is the chief law officer of the Department and serves as legal adviser to the secretarial officers and other officers of the De partment. The Office of the General 

Counsel supervises all legal activities of the Department and supervises and coordinates the development of the Department's legislative program.

The Office of Business Economics provides basic economic measures of the national economy, current analysis of the economic situation and business outlook, the United States balance of international payments, measurement and analysis of the factors affecting regional economic development in the United States, and general economic research on the functioning of the economy. For its analyses the Office develops economic and statistical indicators, and its national income and product work provides a basis for policy formulation by the Department, CREATION AND AUTHORITY.- -The Business and Defense Services Admin istration was established by the Secretary of Commerce on October 1, 1953, by Department Order 152, pursuant to authority of Reorganization Plan 5 of 1950.

Business and Defense Services Administration 

[For regulations codified under this heading, see Code of Federal Reg ulations, Title 15, Chapter VI; Title 19, Chapter III; Title 32A, Chapter VI; Title 44, Chapter IV] ORGANIZATION.-The Administrator of BDSA is responsible to the Assistant 

Secretary for Domestic and International Business. Programs of BDSA are executed by 26 business and industry divisions, grouped by related industries into seven offices. 

FUNCTIONS.-BDSA is in daily con tact with industry and business to keep informed of significant changes and problems confronting the business community and provides active assistance in seven major program areas that directly involve the industry and commerce of the United States.

INDUSTRIAL MODERNIZATION. 

BDSA assesses the effect of industrial change on individual industries. It evaluates the impact of new materials 2002 ala 

other executive agencies, and the Congress, with respect to Government operations insofar as they affect economic movements. Its services to business are long established and well known through the official monthly journal 

Survey of Current Business. The Office of Business Economics organi zation includes six major operating units: National Income Division, Re gional Economics Division, National 

Economics Division, Current Business Analysis Division, Business Structure Division, and the Balance of Payments 

Division. and processes, and the business and economic consequences of changes in industrial practices. BDSA cooperates with industry to broaden awareness of available techniques to increase productivity, employment, and profits through modernization conferences. 

FOREIGN COMMODITY TRADE SUP- 

PORT.-BDSA provides advice and counsel to industries on international business opportunities, tariff questions, commodity problems and market prospects abroad. It contributes to the development of commercial policy by assessing the impact of imports on U.S. industry and implements the Department's responsibilities under the Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Materials Importation Act of 1966 

(Florence Agreement). The Florence 

Agreement facilitates the international free flow of these materials by removing unnecessary trade barriers. 

LEGISLATION AND REGULATION. 

Within the Department's legislative program BDSA initiates and supports

new legislation designed to expand business opportunities in the United 

States, and reviews and recommends. changes in existing regulations to remove burdensome and outdated restrictions on industrial innovation and inventiveness.

GOVERNMENT SERVICES.-BDSA 

helps to develop more meaningful and useful business statistics. It advises other agencies on the nature of business operations to assure fully informed decision making. BDSA prepares data necessary for fruitful and mutually beneficial tariff negotiations. 

GOVERNMENT-BUSINESS 

RELA- TIONS. BDSA assists business to deal effectively with its policy problems involving the Federal Government. It advises Government agencies dealing with business problems about the potential impact of contemplated actions. 

BDSA encourages equal opportunity hiring and promotion in the business community and supports training programs designed to prepare minority groups to gain and hold employment. 

DOMESTIC INDUSTRIAL AND MARKET REPORTING.-BDSA cooperates with business in preparation of special industry studies best performed by a 

Government agency. BDSA works with other Government agencies to collect and distribute business data which industry considers necessary.

INDUSTRIAL MOBILIZATION.-BDSA 

administers the authority delegated to the Secretary of Commerce under the

Defense Production Act of 1950, as amended, with respect to the use of priorities and directives that are necessary to support and expedite the accomplishment of current military, atomic, and space programs through the operation of the Defense Materials 

System. It plans for industrial mobilization and production control in a national emergency, recruits and trains all members of the National Defense Executive Reserve, and provides advice and counsel to the Office of 

Emergency Planning on national stockpile acquisitions, disposals, and specifications.

MAJOR CENSUSES.-The schedule of major censuses regularly taken is: population and housing, once every 10 years for years ending in 0; agriculture, once every 5 years for years ending in 4 and 9, with drainage and irrigation. for years ending in 9; governments, once every 5 years for years ending in 

2 and 7; and manufactures, mineral industries, business, and transportation, generally once every 5 years (dates have varied), scheduled in future for years ending in 2 and 7. 

CURRENT PROGRAMS.-Data col lected at weekly, monthly, quarterly, annual, or other intervals provide upto-date information on most subjects covered in the major censuses, on construction, and on U.S. foreign trade. 

Current programs provide estimates Office and projections of the population; data on population and housing characteristics, including consumer income and buying intentions; measures of activity in manufacturing, retail and wholesale trade, selected services, and construc-: tion; and data on State and local government finances and employment, and on cotton production and distribution.

OTHER SERVICES.-A major activity of the Bureau is conducting surveys for other Federal agencies. Such surveys include the National Health Survey, the survey of employment and unemployment, the survey of expenditures for research and development, and many others.

The Bureau has a large data processing facility for handling statistics from its own censuses and surveys and for assisting other Government agencies with such services at cost. These services include providing computer tapes and punchcards containing machine-readable data, making special tabulations, and assisting in design and alteration of tabulating equipment. 

Machine-readable data and special tabulations are also made available to the public at cost, under appropriate circumstances.

The Bureau has a staff qualified in the fields of sample survey design and methodology and procedural and program planning. This staff performs its functions in Bureau censuses and surveys and acts in an advisory capacity to other Government agencies. 

CREATION AND AUTHORITY.-The Economic Development Administra tion (EDA) was established September 1, 1965, by the Secretary of Commerce pursuant to authority vested in him by the Public Works and Eco nomic Development Act of 1965 (79 

Stat. 552; 42 U.S.C. 3121) and Reorganization Plan 5 of 1950.

The Office of Appalachian Assist ance has been abolished, and its functions administered elsewhere in the 

Economic Development Administra tion. 

The Assistant Secretary for Economic Development is the head of the 

Economic Development Administra tion.

He reports and is responsible to the Secretary of Commerce. 

The Bureau also provides statistical consultation to foreign governments, orientation programs for foreign visitors, and training for foreign technicians. 

Economic Development Administration 

Regulations, Title 13, Chapter III; Title 44, Chapter VIII] 

Special censuses in local areas are taken at the request and expense of the local governments. 

Searches are made of the decennial census records of population and certificates furnished to individuals for use as evidence of age and place of birth. 

A fee is charged for the searches. 

A list of major statistical series published by the Bureau is provided in appendix B of this volume. The Bureau of the Census Catalog, issued quarterly and cumulated to the annual volume, contains an annotated listing of publications and a subject and geographical index to their contents and an annotated list of machine-readable data files and unpublished materials available in the Bureau of the Census. 

PURPOSE. The primary function assigned EDA by statute is the longrange economic development and programing for areas and regions of substantial and persistent unemployment and underemployment and low family income through the creation of new employment opportunities by developing new and expanding existing facilities and resources in such areas and regions.

CREATION AND AUTHORITY.-The Environmental Science Services Ad ministration (ESSA) was established on July 13, 1965, through the consolidation of the Coast and Geodetic Survey and the Weather Bureau in accordance with the provisions of Reorganization Plan 2 of 1965. As provided by Department of Commerce Order 2-A, as amended, the Central Radio Propagation Laboratory, the Geoacoustics Group, and the Office of Radio Frequency Management of the National Bureau of Standards were transferred to the Administration. Authority to perform the functions included under title 15, chapter 9, U.S. 

Code (Weather Bureau), title 33, chapter 17, U.S. Code (Coast and 

Geodetic Survey), and all other authority contained in legislation, Executive order, etc., pertaining to the consolidated organizations has been delegated to the Administration. 

PURPOSE. The mission of ESSA is to describe, understand, and predict the state of the oceans, the state of the EDA exercises program control and provides policy direction in furnishing such aid in close collaboration with other Federal agencies.

The Administration's area offices and representatives provide direct assistance to State and local agencies concerned with, and engaged in, economic development activities.

Bureau of International Commerce  Reg ulations, Title 15, Chapter III] CREATION AND AUTHORITY.-The 

Bureau of International Commerce (BIC), center of the Department's international commercial activities, was established by the Secretary on February 1, 1963, by Department Order 182, under authority provided by Reorganization Plan 5 of 1950.

BIC promotes the foreign trade of the United States and assists U.S. business in its operations abroad.

PURPOSE. The prime objective of the Bureau is to increase U.S. exports. 

This contributes to the Nation's economic growth and helps to reduce the deficit in the U.S. balance of international payments. To carry out this objective, BIC: (1) provides services and information to American businessmen to help them trade abroad; (2) operates overseas trade centers, sends trade missions abroad, stages commercial exhibitions at international trade fairs, and provides other marketing services. to promote the sale of U.S. goods abroad; (3) works with other Government agencies and international organizations to improve conditions for international trade and investment; (4) presents the views of traders and investors in governmental councils; and (5) works out policies and procedures to make doing business abroad simpler and more profitable. cial personnel serving abroad in the Foreign Service under the jurisdiction of the Department of State; and (6) develops guidelines covering the functions and responsibilities of economic/ commercial officers abroad, and initiates or coordinates instructions to overseas posts.

The Bureau also administers the Export Control Act of 1949, as amended (50 U.S.C., App. 2021, 2024) to prevent the export of strategic U.S. materials, equipment, and technical data to Sino-Soviet bloc countries where their use could be detrimental to the 

United States.

In addition, it administers the China Trade Act of 1922, as amended (15 U.S.C. 141 et seq.) to promote U.S. exports to Hong Kong and Taiwan. 

ORGANIZATION.-BIC is headed by a Director who is responsible to the 

Assistant Secretary for Domestic and 

International Business.

The Office of the Director includes the Compliance Commissioner, the Executive Secretariat of the Advisory Committee on Export Policy, the Executive Secretariat of the Foreign- Trade Zones Board, and the International Organizations Staff. There are five other Offices in the Bureau: Commercial and Financial Policy, Interna tional Regional Economics, Interna tional Trade Promotion, International 

Investment, and Export Control.

FUNCTIONS AND ACTIVITIES 

30 

COMMERCIAL AND FINANCIAL POL- 

ICY. BIC develops and recommends the Department's international commercial and financial policies and programs.

In the field of trade and commercial policy, BIC contributes to international trade negotiations; advises the President's Special Representative for Trade Negotiations on business interest in reduction of foreign tariff and other trade barriers; and participates

in developing U.S. courses of action in the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), the Organization for 

Economic Cooperation and Develop ment (OECD), and the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD). BIC also conducts studies and makes recommendations on legislative and administrative actions concerning specific changes in tariffs, other import restrictions, and other measures relating to the impact of imports on the domestic economy.

In the field of international resources, BIC contributes to international discussions pertaining to international commodities and material policies, marketing arrangements, and commodity groups. 

In the field of foreign business practices, BIC proposes revisions of U.S. 

Government policies, regulations, and procedures to maintain the competitiveness of U.S. firms in international operations; recommends action counteract arbitrary and discriminatory treatment of American business; and reconciles business needs with U.S. policy aims in this field. 

In the field of international finance, BIC presents the American business viewpoint in developing policies for loans and views on specific loans made by the Export-Import Bank, Agency for International Development, and international lending organizations, and proposes and reviews policies promoting U.S. private investment in less developed countries. 234-298-67-21 to In the field of transportation and insurance, BIC assures consideration of export expansion in the development of transportation policy by Government agencies, makes recommendations concerning discriminatory ocean freight rates and other transportation cost factors adversely affecting exports, provides staff support to the interagency National Facilitation Committee; and provides advice and assistance to U.S. business on questions relating to internationl insurance. 

INTERNATIONAL REGIONAL ECONOM- 

ICS. BIC provides businessmen with information on marketing, investment, and economic conditions in more than a hundred countries and regions to help them find new business abroad. 

It helps businessmen determine their export potentials by supplying them with data on conditions or policies affecting their ability to compete in particular markets, prepares statistical analyses on trade between the United States and other countries as well as among foreign countries, and is the primary source for analyses of trade statistics of foreign countries. 

BIC also works with the U.S. Foreign Service to remove foreign governments' trade restrictions which make it difficult for U.S. exporters to compete in overseas markets.

INTERNATIONAL TRADE 

PROMO- TION. BIC operates trade centers, presents exhibitions at international trade fairs, conducts the trade missions program, and provides basic commercial information on firms to facilitate international trade.

U.S. trade centers located in London, Frankfurt, Bangkok, Tokyo, Milan, and Stockholm are permanent show-and-sell facilities in overseas marketing areas where interest in buying U.S.-made goods is combined with purchasing power.

U.S. commercial exhibitions are staged at international trade fairs abroad to open new markets for U.S. products and to secure overseas agencies for future business. 

U.S. trade missions, consisting of selected U.S. businessmen, are sent into promising world markets to develop sales and business opportunities for U.S. firms. 

Mobile trade fairs are containerized exhibits in ships, planes, or vans organized by private organizations to show and sell U.S. products overseas. 

Sample product displays are operated by U.S. commercial officers in 

Nairobi, Beirut, Manila, and Bangkok to assist U.S. firms, particularly those

MARVARD LO 

new to the market and new to export, to find distributors for their products in these markets.

Other business services provided by 

BIC include: Commercial intelligence to help U.S. firms locate potential customers or representatives overseas; assistance in obtaining foreign distributors, importers, and agents; assistance, with the cooperation of the Foreign Service, in settling trade disputes between U.S. and foreign firms; and the maintenance of an automated American International Traders Index to provide businessmen with rapid access to BIC services. 

INTERNATIONAL INVESTMENT.-BIC 

identifies investment opportunities in the developing countries and brings them to the attention of U.S. business, encourages firms abroad to make investments in the United States, especially in areas of heavy unemployment, promotes the licensing of foreign technology to American firms, and publishes for the benefit of American industry opportunities for investment and licensing ventures in the industrialized countries of the free world.

CREATION AND AUTHORITY.-The 

Maritime Administration was established by Reorganization Plan 21 of 

1950, effective May 24, 1950, as one of the successor agencies to the former 

United States Maritime Commission.

EXPORT CONTROL.-BIC administers the export control program: (1) to keep unfriendly nations from obtaining U.S. commodities or technical data that would contribute significantly to their military or economic potential to the detriment of U.S. security or welfare; (2) to protect the U.S. economy against excessive drain of scarce materials; and (3) to further the foreign policy of the United States. BIC also conducts educational programs to enlist support of the U.S. business community for effective export control and investigates suspected violations of export regulations and develops evidence.  Reg ulations, Title 32A, Chapter XVIII (National Shipping Authority) and XIX (Office of the Maritime Administrator); Title 46, Chapter II (Maritime Administration and Maritime Subsidy Board)] PURPOSE.-The Maritime Adminis tration administers programs authorized by the Merchant Marine Act, 1936, as amended, and related shipping statutes to aid in the development, promotion, and operation of the U.S. merchant marine, so that it will be (a) adequate to carry the Nation's domestic waterborne commerce and a substantial portion of its foreign commerce during peacetime; (b) capable of serving as a naval and military auxiliary in time of war or national emergency; (c) owned and operated under U.S. flag by citizens of the United States, so far as may be practicable; and (d) composed of the best equipped, safest, and most suitable types of ships manned by a trained and efficient citizen personnel. 

ORGANIZATION.-The Maritime Ad ministration is headed by a Maritime Administrator, who is appointed by the President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate. Its headquarters organization in Washington, D.C., is composed of the following 

Offices: Program Planning, Budget and Management, Public Information, Data Systems, Personnel Management, General Counsel, Comptroller, Prop erty and Supply, Ship Construction, Research and Development, Ship Operations, Government Aid, Maritime

Maritime Administration a Maritime 

Subsidy Board, composed of the Maritime Administrator, who serves 

Chairman, the Deputy Maritime Ad ministrator, and the General Counsel, each of whom acts pursuant to direct authority from the Secretary of Commerce. The Board makes, amends, and terminates contracts for operating-differential and construction-differential subsidies. It conducts hearings and makes determinations antecedent to these actions; and it investigates and determines the relative costs of constructing ships in the United States and in foreign countries and of operating ships under United States and competitive foreign flags. 

The Maritime Administrator is also vested with the residual powers and authorities of the Director, National Shipping Authority, which was established by the Secretary of Commerce on March 13, 1951, for the purpose of organizing and directing emergency merchant ship operations in the national interest. 

In the districts, the Offices of the 

Atlantic, Gulf, and Pacific Coast Directors located at New York, N.Y., New Orleans, La., and San Francisco,

Calif., are responsible for all field offices and programs of the Maritime Administration within their respective coast areas, except ship construction and maritime training.

In addition, the Administration insures mortgages and/or loans made by private lending institutions to finance. the construction, reconstruction, and reconditioning of ships; and it acquires old ships in exchange for more modern and efficient ships or for allowances of credit on the construction of new ships.

GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE TO SHIP- PING. The Maritime Administration administers the operating-differential and construction-differential subsidy programs and other Government aids to merchant shipping, authorized by law. Under these programs, the Government pays the difference between certain costs of operating ships under U.S.-flag and foreign competitive flags, on essential foreign trade routes; and the difference (not to exceed a certain The Administration also investigates and determines ocean services, routes, and lines essential for the development and maintenance of the foreign commerce of the United 

States; and the type, size, speed, and other requirements of ships to provide adequate service on such routes. The operators who are awarded operatingdifferential subsidy contracts are required to maintain regular services on these routes.

The Administration assists the shipping industry to generate increased trade and cargo shipments for U.S.-flag ships. Shippers, freight forwarders, and manufacturers are encouraged to use U.S.-flag shipping in conformance with sections 101 and 212(d) of the act of 1936, as an aid to U.S. merchant marine, and to assist in developing a credit position in balance of payments. 

RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT. 

The Maritime Administration con ducts research and development activities in the maritime field, including lization of new ship designs, marine cargo handling, development and utitransportation systems, advanced propulsion concepts, and ship mechanization and management techniques. The objectives of this program are to improve the efficiency and economy of operations of the American merchant marine and to promote more rapid technical advancement of it.

SHIPBUILDING AND 

DESIGN.-The Maritime Administration develops plans and specifications for prototype ships. It encourages and participates in the development of plans and designs by subsidized operators under their ship replacement programs, and by applicants for Government aid covering ships proposed to be constructed or converted. It inspects ships during the course of work to assure conformance with approved plans and specifications. 

To carry out the national maritime policy, the Maritime Administration, with the approval of the President, constructs, reconstructs, and reconditions ships for Government account. 

The Administration is authorized to sell these ships, charter them to private operators, or utilize them for Government operation.

SHIP OPERATIONS AND REPAIR.- The Maritime Administration charters 

Government-owned ships to United States operators when it is determined that such charters will promote the national maritime policy. During national emergencies it requisitions or procures for operation or for charter ships owned by citizens of the United States or under construction, and it determines requirements for and allocates ships to meet the needs of national defense programs. It reactivates 

Government-owned ships from the national defense reserve fleets and operates them, through general agents, Baltimore, Md.

CREATION AND AUTHORITY.- -The 

Patent Office was established to administer the patent laws enacted by Congress in accordance with Article I, section 8, of the Constitution. The first of these laws was enacted April 10, 1790 (1 Stat. 109). General revisions of the patent laws were made on 

July 4, 1836 (5 Stat. 117), and on 

July 8, 1870 (16 Stat. 198). These and other acts of Congress relating to patents were revised and codified, effective January 1, 1953, by the act of 

July 19, 1952 (66 Stat. 792; 35 U.S.C. 

1-293). In addition to the patent laws, the Patent Office administers the 

Federal trademark laws, the present statute being the act approved July 5, 1946 (60 Stat. 427; 15 U.S.C. 1051, as amended).

WAR RISK INSURANCE. The Mari time Administration is authorized to provide Government war risk insurance of merchant ships, their cargoes and crews, when adequate insurance cannot be obtained on reasonable terms and conditions from private insurance companies in the United States.

ACTIVITIES.—The Patent Office examines applications for patents to ascertain if the applicants are entitled to patents under the law, and grants the patents when they are so entitled; it publishes and disseminates patented matter, records the assignment of patents, maintains a Scientific Library and a search file of U.S. and foreign patents for public use, and supplies copies of patents and official records of the Patent Office. Office of State Technical Services (Washington, D.C.) 

 Reg ulations, Title 15, Chapter VII] CREATION AND AUTHORITY.-The Office of State Technical Services was established by Departmental Order 7A 

of November 19, 1965, pursuant to the act of September 14, 1965 (79 Stat. 

679; 15 U.S.C. 1351), to administer and coordinate the State Technical Services program. 

PURPOSE. The purpose of State 

Technical Services is to promote commerce and encourage economic growth by supporting State and interstate programs to place the findings of science usefully in the hands of American enterprise.

OGY. This institute provides for the creation of appropriate opportunities for the use and application of technology within the Federal Government and within the civilian sector of American industry. The primary functions of the Institute may be broadly classified as programs relating to technical information and measurement programs related to the use of technology. 

ORGANIZATION.-The Office of State 

Technical Services is responsible for the actual administration and coordi nation of the State Technical Services 

Act of 1965.

OSTS consists of the 

Director's Office, Special Programs Di vision, State Programs Division, and 

Reference Services Division. All tech nical services to business, commerce, and industry are provided at the local level through State programs. 

CREATION.-The United States Travel Service was established June 

29, 1961, pursuant to the International 

Travel Act of 1961 (75 Stat. 129; 22 ACTIVITIES.-The State Technical Services Act permits Federal grants to all 50 States, the District of Columbia, Guam, Puerto Rico, and the Virgin

Islands. The Governor of each State or 

Territory must designate an agency to administer and coordinate the technical services program in that State. Each designated agency is eligible to receive a planning grant of up to $25,000 for each of the first 3 years. The designated agency must prepare a comprehensive 5-year plan and an annual technical services program to receive an annual Federal grant in support of the State program. The program grant must be matched by State or non-Federal funds. The technical services are performed primarily by the State universities or colleges.

The act also authorizes matching grants in support of technical services programs which have special merit.. 

Such programs should normally benefit two or more States or the Nation as a whole.

PURPOSE. The purposes of the

Travel Service are to develop, plan, and carry out a comprehensive program designed to stimulate and encourage travel to the United States by residents of foreign countries for the purpose of study, culture, recreation, business, and other activities as a means of promoting friendly understanding and good will among peoples of foreign countries and of the United States; encourage the development of tourist facilities, low-cost unit tours, and other arrangements within the United States for meeting the requirements of foreign visitors; foster and encourage the widest possible distribution of the benefits of travel at the cheapest rates between foreign countries and the United States consistent with sound economic principles; encourage the simplification, reduction, or elimination of barriers to travel, and the facilitation of international travel generally; collect, publish, and provide for the exchange of statistics and technical information, including schedules of meetings, fairs, and other attractions, relating to international travel and tourism.

ORGANIZATION.-The program of the Travel Service is conducted by the following divisions: Travel Promotion, 

Facilitation and Planning, and Visitor Services. In addition to these divisions, eleven overseas offices have been established to stimulate tourist travel. These offices are located in London, England; 

Paris, France; Frankfurt, Germany;

Rome, Italy; Tokyo, Japan; Sydney, Australia; São Paulo, Brazil; Caracas, Venezuela; Mexico City, Mexico; 

Amsterdam, Netherlands; and Stockholm, Sweden.

ACTIVITIES.-The major share of appropriated funds are used to provide tools and materials for distribution by the overseas offices, such as advertisements, pamphlets, brochures, posters, slides, and films, in order to help the prospective traveler study and measure the United States against other competitive destinations. 

In addition, the following activities are being carried out: editorial support of the program through domestic and foreign media endorsing the 

United States as a tourist destination; encouragement to State and local community groups for the establishment of "host" services throughout the country; development of ways and means of overcoming barriers to travel; and a study of the economic aspects of tourism and patterns of international travel. Approved.

CREATION AND AUTHORITY.-The Department of Labor, ninth executive department, was created by act ap proved March 4, 1913 (37 Stat. 

736; 5 U.S.C. 611). A Bureau of

Labor was first created by Congress in 1884 under the Interior Department. The Bureau of Labor later became independent as a Department of Labor without executive rank. It again returned to bureau status in the De partment of Commerce and Labor which was created by act of February 

14, 1903 (32 Stat. 827; 5 U. S. C. 591).

Additional duties related to the statutory functions of the Department of Labor subsequently have been assigned Appeals

PURPOSE.-The Department of La bor is charged, among other things, with administering and enforcing statutes designed to advance the public interest by promoting the welfare of the wage earners of the United States, improving their working conditions, and advancing their opportunities for profitable employment.

OFFICE OF INFORMATION, PUBLICA TIONS, AND REPORTS.-The Director of Information, Publications, and Reports plans and directs all informational activities of the Department, advises the Secretary on the public information aspect of the Department's programs, and develops and maintains

appropriate liaison with other agencies and organizations and with foreign countries in connection with the work of the Department. He supervises departmental relations with press, radio, television, and other public information media, and is clearance officer for all Labor Department issuances. 

OFFICE OF POLICY PLANNING AND RESEARCH. -The Director of Policy 

Planning and Research is responsible for providing leadership in the development of policies and programs needed to promote the welfare of all workers; developing program projections for future periods, recommending new programs and changes in existing programs, and identifying programs or activities for which new legislative authority may be required; developing and coordinating research programs throughout the Department; and planning processes under the Department's Management System (which includes all the requirements of the Government-wide Planning-Programing-Budgeting System). He is the focal point of responsibility for initiating policy planning and research and for forwarding recommendations to the Secretary.

OFFICE OF FEDERAL CONTRACT COM- PLIANCE. The Office of Federal Con tract Compliance administers Execu tive Order 11246, parts II, III and IV, which require that equal employment opportunity be provided by Government contractors and subcontractors and on federally-assisted construction projects. The Office provides Federal policy; assists and guides Federal contracting agencies and contractors; develops procedures for the optimum overall use of agency resources; monitors contracting agency compliance programs for adequacy and consistency; and coordinates with the Equal 

Employment Opportunity Commis sion and other related governmental and private agencies and interested parties to carry out the objectives of the 

Executive order with fair and uniform treatment of contractors and their employees. 

The Under Secretary of Labor is the alternate of the Secretary in the discharge of all the Secretary's responsibilities. He serves as Acting Secretary in the Secretary's absence.

Assistant Secretary for Manpower 

The Assistant Secretary for Man power has responsibility for all the De- 

Manpower Administration 

The Manpower Administration is composed of the immediate office of the Manpower Administrator, including the President's Committee on Manpower and the National Manpower Advisory Committee, and the following offices and bureaus: 

Office of Financial and Management 

Services

The Office directs all Manpower Administration activities in the areas of budget, fund control, personnel management, management analysis, contracting services, and administrative services. It serves as the principal adviser to the Manpower Administrator on the status of funds under the Administrator's responsibility and serves as the point of coordination for all administrative management matters within the Manpower Administration. 

Office of Manpower Policy, Evaluation and Research partment manpower programs and activities.

This office performs planning, research, and evaluation functions. It develops and recommends plans for a comprehensive national manpower program that will guide and make possible the coordination of decisions and activities of the Department of Labor, and in addition provide guidelines for other Federal agencies, employers, labor unions, professional organizations, State and local governments (including those engaged in educational activity), private educational institutions, and others in making and executing manpower decisions. This includes the development of policies and standards for implementing such manpower development and utilization programs as enumerated above. 

The Office appraises the manpower requirements and resources of the Nation and develops policies, objectives, and standards to deal with the problems of persistent and other types of unemployment and underemployment, while considering such factors as current and prospective manpower shortages, dislocations in the economy arising from automation or other technological developments, foreign competition, relocation of industry, shifts in market demands, and other changes in the structure of the economy. 

The Office provides leadership in planning, evaluating, and coordinating manpower the and automation research and related statistic programs in the Department and identifies the need for and plans, conducts, or arranges for other bureaus of the Department or other Government or private agencies to conduct high-priority, pathfinding research to augment existing research in the manpower area. The objective is to identify the many ramifications and the dimensions of the manpower problems of the Nation and to seek through research, adequate solutions to these problems. It plans and directs developmental and experimental studies in all areas of manpower and automation to find solutions to problems which significantly affect the Nation's ability to eliminate persistent and other types of unemployment and underemployment and to evaluate the impact of and benefits and problems created by automation and other forms of technological progress. It plans and develops a program to increase and expand knowledge of how occupational competence that will aid in eliminating unemployment and underemployment is achieved.

The Office prepares materials for the President's and the Secretary of Labor's annual manpower reports together with recommendations for action. It provides technical manpower information to the public, professional groups, unions, employers, and Government agencies on the nature of manpower problems and programs. It maintains a clearinghouse of technical and research information on manpower, automation, and training. 

The Office coordinates the program planning and development activities of the Department of Labor bureaus providing manpower programs for the aging, minority groups, the handicapped, and youth, and insures that the bureaus and offices providing manpower programs take into account the occupational interests, circumstances, and operations of women in the labor force.

The Office promotes and develops experimental and demonstration manpower projects through contracts with public and private organizations for special worker groups with emphasis on disadvantaged persons, unique or emerging occupations and operating programs which are national or regional in character; develops objectives, policies, and standards governing such projects; and contracts with col- Region leges and universities to conduct followup studies to determine whether the programs are meeting the occupational training needs of those they serve. It has the prime responsibility for converting experimental and demonstration results to operational policies and procedures for use by governmental agencies with manpower responsibilities.

The Bureau promotes the establishment and improvement of apprenticeship and other on-the-job training programs and provides technical assistance and training aids where necessary. Its functions are to aid management and labor in recognizing the need for apprenticeship. Through field representatives in each State the Bureau works closely with employers, labor, vocational schools, and others concerned with apprenticeship programs throughout industry. Programs must meet standards established by the Federal Committee on Apprenticeship to be registered with the Bureau.

The Bureau has responsibility for on-the-job training under the Man power Development and Training 

Act. Agreements are made with employers, labor unions, associations, and public agencies to conduct training programs using the facilities of such groups to train the unemployed, underemployed, and those whose skills have become or are becoming obsolete. On-the-job training under this program may be combined with supplemental technical instruction by agreement with public schools. 

Bureau of Employment Security 

[For regulations codified under this head ing, see Code of Federal Regulations, Title 20, Chapter V] 

The Bureau's responsibilities are related to the administration of a nationwide system of public employment services, State unemployment insurance programs, Federal unemployment compensation programs, and special manpower programs designed to relieve the effects of unemployment and to promote maximum utilization of the Nation's manpower. The legislative bases for the Bureau's operations include the Wagner-Peyser Act, the 

Federal Unemployment Tax Act, titles III, IX, XII, and XV of the Social Security Act, the Farm Labor Contrac tor Registration Act, various provisions in the Immigration and National ity Act, the Automotive Products Trade Act, the Public Works and Economic Development Act, the Manpower Development and Training Act, the Vocational Education Act of 1963, the Trade Expansion Act, the Eco nomic Opportunity Act, and the Civil 

Rights Act. 

The Bureau coordinates employment security activities with other Government agencies and the public, and advises the legislative and executive branches on employment security matters. It plans programs on a nationwide basis. To facilitate sound program planning, it collects and analyzes operational and economic data related to employment security programs, which in published form provide Government, labor, management, and the public with information of value in assessing economic trends and developments.

The Bureau conducts evaluations of the administration and operation of 

State employment security agencies. 

This involves the measurement of achievements, the making of recommendations for improving State administrative operations and management, and the provision of assistance in the establishment of improved methods of administration and operation. 

Fiscal responsibilities involve determination of funds needed and justification of appropriation requests before Congress, allocation of funds among States, establishment of standards for expenditures, filing of exceptions on funds improperly expended, review of applicable State laws and their execution, and certification of laws which

meet Federal requirements to permit the allocation of Federal funds for administrative costs.

The Bureau provides leadership to the State employment security agencies, involving responsibility to: (1) develop and interpret national policies and goals; (2) study program needs and administrative problems; (3) develop techniques, tools, and measures for improvement in administration and program content; (4) promote adoption of improvements in State legislation and administration; and (5) provide continuing technical assistance and interchange of experience and information.

The Bureau works closely with State agencies in the development and maintenance of a well-selected and trained staff. 

The Bureau coordinates nationwide developmental projects designed to provide tools, methods, and material for adaptive use throughout the employment security system. From such coordinated efforts have come such products as the Dictionary of Occupational Titles, occupational tests, and occupational job descriptions. 

its United States Employment Service under the provisions of the Wagner- Peyser Act, include assistance in establishing and maintaining a system of public employment offices in the States and territories; assistance in coordinating the system throughout the country and increasing its usefulness by developing and prescribing minimum standards of efficiency; collecting and furnishing information as to opportunities for employment and other information of value in operating the system, including information about labor area developments by industry and occupation and classification of certain areas according to relative labor supply; maintaining a public employment service for the District of Columbia, a veterans' service devoted to obtaining employment for veterans, and a placement service for agriculture and its workers; and maintaining a system for interarea recruitment of labor among the States. The United States Employ ment Service guides and assists the State agencies in placement functions, occupational analysis, counseling, and testing functions; in maximizing employment opportunities for veterans, older workers, youth, handicapped workers, members of minority groups, and workers affected by the impact of automation and changing technology; in promoting community efforts toward the greatest possible use of the labor force; in providing employers with information about the skills of public employment service applicants and in finding job opportunities for applicants; and in providing materials and techniques to employers for effective use of manpower. The Employment Service assists State agencies in providing a full range of services to rural areas and small communities. In many States mobile teams of counselors, interviewers, and test administrators extend these services. 

The Bureau cooperates with other offices of the Department and with other Federal agencies in the war on poverty, especially in developing employability among culturally, educationally, and economically deprived youth. It is responsible under title VI of the Civil Rights Act for insuring that the Federal-State employment security program is administered without discrimination on the basis of race, color, or country of origin.

The Bureau also actively participates in manpower mobilization planning and in the preparation being made by the Federal Government for national emergencies which might arise. In addition, the Bureau coordinates civil defense and mobilization activities in State employment security agencies.

The Office of Farm Labor Service develops policies and procedures to 

TEADWADD TOW LIBRARY

provide a complete placement service to workers and employers in the agricultural, food processing, and woods industries. It directs and coordinates this service to insure that year-round and seasonal labor requirements of agriculture are met and that individual workers seeking employment in agriculture are exposed to all available job opportunities. It seeks to provide an orderly, expeditious, seasonal movement of migrant workers to successive jobs through interstate clearance and the Annual Worker Plan by maintain ing current, reliable information regarding crop conditions and employment opportunities. It operates seasonal farm programs for special groups such as high school and college youth, reservation Indians, and Puerto Ri cans. The Office of Farm Labor Service is responsible for insuring that in the interstate recruitment of farmworkers applicable standards and the Secretary's regulations are met relating to housing, transportation, wages, and other conditions. It also provides for 

Federal registration of interstate farm labor contractors. The office reviews and makes determinations on requests for the importation and employment of alien farmworkers under the Immigration and Nationality Act. It determines the need for training in farm skills, recruits potential trainees, and attempts to place graduate trainees. 

The Bureau's unemployment insurance program responsibilities assigned to its Unemployment Insurance Service include review and analysis of State laws to determine if they are in con formity with the Social Security Act, the Federal Unemployment Tax Act, and regulations of the Secretary of 

Labor; review of State administration of unemployment insurance to determine whether the program is operating in compliance with Federal requirements, and whether individuals are denied benefits to which they are entitled under the State law and under the various agreements with the Secretary of Labor to carry out the Federal

Unemployment Compensation programs for former Federal civilian employees and ex-servicemen; establishment of feasible criteria for determining the amounts of money necessary for proper and efficient administration of the State unemployment compensation laws; and furnishing assistance to the States on administrative and operating problems on program and financial reserves, and in developing legislative recommendations designed to improve the program under the economy of each State. The Bureau also analyzes data on unemployment compensation coverage, contributions, benefit rights, and benefit payments State by State and for the Nation as a whole; studies and recommends methods of improving the unemployment insurance program; disseminates information on the operation of the program; prepares evaluations of the adequacy of the States' unemployment insurance benefit funds, and tax structures; reviews applications for advances (loans) from the Federal Unemployment Account, and certifies (for the Secretary of Labor) to the Secretary of the

Treasury the amount of such advance to which the State is eligible under title XII of the Social Security Act; 

studies and develops policy recommendations concerning other governmental or private income-maintenance programs which may affect the unemployment insurance system; arranges with 

State employment security agencies for payment of training allowances under the Manpower Development and 

Training Act, of readjustment allowances under the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 and of relocation allowances, as grants or loans under the Manpower 

Development and Training Act or the Trade Expansion Act of 1962. 

The Federal Advisory Council on 

Employment Security, composed of representatives of employers, employees, and the public, was established by the Wagner-Peyser Act "to

discuss problems and develop policy recommendations relating to employment and unemployment, and to insure impartiality, neutrality, and freedom from political influence in the solution of such problems." The Coun cil advises the Secretary of Labor and the Administrator of the Bureau with respect to the administration and coordination of the functions of the Bureau.

Bureau of Work Programs The Bureau of Work Programs is re sponsible for administering youth and adult programs which offer a broad range of work-experience, training, and career-related services in rural and urban centers. Each program has a slightly different format geared to meet the varying needs of individual participants. The programs are titled the 

Neighborhood Youth Corps; Special 

Impact, designed for both youth and adults; and Operation Mainstream and New Careers, both designed for adult participation. 

NEIGHBORHOOD YOUTH CORPS.- 

Oldest of the programs is the Neighborhood Youth Corps, which was authorized by the Economic Opportunity 

Act of 1964 (78 Stat. 508; 42 U.S.C. 

2701), as amended. 

The purpose of this part of the antipoverty program is to make it possible for young people to remain in school, to return to school, to gain useful work experience, to earn an income, and to receive the special training and careerrelated services that will help them develop their maximum occupational potential. to develop their maximum occupational potential.

Eligible for in-school projects are young men and women who attend school as well as those who have dropped out of school but intend to return. All in-school enrollees must come from families with annual incomes below the poverty-line and must be in need of earnings to permit them to resume or maintain attendance in school. In-school projects may include students in grades 9 through 12, those who attend elementary school and are at least 14 years of age, and recent dropouts who are at least 14 years of age. Special provisions must be included in proposals that provide for enrollment of any persons below 16 years of age. 

Persons who fulfill the requirements for in-school projects are eligible for summer projects.

Priority in out-of-school projects will be given to young men and women from families with annual incomes below the poverty-line. These enrollees must have dropped out of school at least 3 months prior to enrollment, have no immediate plans to return to school, and must be unemployed, be 

16 through 21 years of age (although individuals already enrolled who reach 

22 years of age can be permitted to remain in the project until they reach the age of 23). They must also need work-experience and, in some cases, job-related supportive services.

There are three types of projects: inschool, out-of-school, and summer. 

Work assignments in both the public and private sector provide experience in many fields, including education, conservation, health, food service, community and public service, and recreation. Priority is given to projects that offer all enrollees the best opportunity 

An enrollee may stay in an in-school project until graduation from high school. The period of enrollment in out-of-school projects is limited to 2 years.

SPECIAL IMPACT.-Special Impact is the name given by Congress to special programs, authorized by a 1966 

amendment (title I-D) to the 1964 

Equal Opportunity Act, for both youths and adults, whose goal is to solve critical problems facing specific urban areas with large numbers of lowincome residents. 1

HARVAND LO!! 

These projects are to serve as catalysts for developing and mobilizing all resources within a community that can play a part in reducing chronic unemployment, eliminating tensions, and generally improving the overall environment of a particular urban neighborhood. 

With coordination of all Federal,

State, and local resources that can provide manpower training, education, health, and community planning services, the projects will concentrate on work training that will result in improvement in the neighborhoods where participants live.

Project activities may include renovating houses or apartments, improving health facilities, developing vest pocket parks, expanding community programs, and developing recreational facilities. 

Priority will go to those projects that provide a total spectrum of services and therefore appear most likely to help participants obtain permanent jobs.

Preferred applicants are the chronically unemployed who have no reasonable prospects for full-time employment or for training assistance under other Federal training programs. Those eligible must be residents of the community or neighborhood served by the project, be at least 16 years of age, and either come from families whose annual income falls below the poverty line or be unemployed. 

Projects must be located in urban neighborhoods with large concentrations of low-income persons. Priority is given to projects that demonstrate optimum linkage and coordination with all other related programs; provide training not otherwise available to residents of the neighborhood; and involve neighborhood residents both as planners and participants.

OPERATION MAINSTREAM.-Opera tion Mainstream, authorized by a 1965 

amendment (title II, sec. 205 (d)) to the Economic Opportunity Act, is the second oldest program currently operating within the Bureau of Work Programs and is geared for community betterment and beautification. It was formerly administered by the Office of Economic Opportunity and was designated as "Nelson Programs," with some rural projects referred to as "Green Thumb.”

Operation Mainstream seeks to provide permanent jobs, at decent wages, for adults with a history of chronic unemployment. Designed for rural areas and towns, projects concentrate on work-experience and training activities that will improve communities and those low-income areas where the projects take place. 

Among other things, such projects may seek to decrease air and water pollution, improve parks, protect wildlife, rehabilitate slum housing, or extend education, health, and social services. 

Any agency that requests the services of an enrollee must give reasonable assurance that it can offer to that en rollee future full-employment, independent of financial support from the 

Bureau of Work Programs (BWP). 

Priority will be given to those per sons who have been chronically unemployed; those who lack current prospects for training or employment because of age or otherwise; or those who have completed some training but remain unemployed. To be eligible, individuals must be at least 22 years of age and come from a family with an annual income below the poverty line. 

Preferred projects are those that lead to opportunities for permanent employment; provide services, or employment for older persons in rural areas or towns; and improve the social or physical environment in areas of concentrated poverty.

NEW CAREERS.-New Careers is a program authorized under a 1966 amendment (title II, sec. 205(e)) to the Economic Opportunity Act. 

The goal of this program is to establish on a permanent basis new and necessary community service jobs. As a pioneering effort, this program seeks

to demonstrate that the restructuring of professional jobs, in both public and private enterprise, will result in improved services, more efficient utilization of professionally-trained persons, and purposeful, dignified employment for those now unemployed. 12 The program is designed to meet critical local shortages, both current and projected, of professional personnel in such essential fields as health, education, and public safety by reengineering professional jobs, extracting tasks that require less than professional training, and establishing specifications for new jobs to fulfill these tasks. 

The program also opens up additional career avenues by setting up realistic entry-level requirements and by making possible progression to better paying and more responsible jobs. 

Projects will take place in communities where maximum prospects for future career opportunities exist. 

Priority will be given to projects that not only ease the workload of profes- Isionals but also lead to the creation of permanent new jobs, with opportunities for advancement in fields that will benefit the poor. Projects will be expected to demonstrate that permanent jobs will exist at the same or higher levels for persons who complete work training. 卫 ​To be eligible, an individual must be

Wage and Hour and Public Contracts Divisions 

[For regulations codified under this head ing, see Code of Federal Regulations, Title 29, Chapter V; Title 41, Chapter 50] The Wage and Hour Division was established pursuant to the provisions of the Fair Labor Standards Act of 

June 25, 1938 (52 Stat. 1060; 29

U.S.C. 201-219). The Public Con tracts Division was created to admin ister the Walsh-Healey Public Contracts Act of June 30, 1936 (49 Stat. 

2036; 41 U.S.C. 35-45). The two Divisions were consolidated by order of the Secretary of Labor on August 21, 1942. The Wage and Hour and Public Contracts Divisions are headed by an 

Administrator, appointed by the President with the consent of the Senate. 

The Fair Labor Standards Act, ernment supply contracts in amounts exceeding $10,000 to contain certain stipulations concerning labor standards and conditions of work. WHPC administers and enforces contract provisions pertaining to the payment of prevailing minimum wages and overtime, and non-employment of child and convict labor. WHPC also administers and enforces the prevailing minimum wage and fringe benefit provisions of the Mc- 

Namara-O'Hara Service Contract Act of 1965, which applies to Federal Government contracts for services which exceed $2,500. All employees performing work under service contracts, including contracts of $2,500 or less, must be paid at least the minimum wage provided by the Fair Labor Standards 

Act. In addition, WHPC administers and enforces the prevailing wage provisions of the National Foundation on the Arts and the Humanities Act applicable to grants-in-aid for the arts. 

WHPC's national office develops policies and programs, issues regulations and interpretations, conducts economic research, develops certification standards for learners, apprentices, full-time students, and handicapped workers, establishes prevailing minimum wage rates under the Public 

Contracts Act and the Service Con tract Act, coordinates the enforcement program, and directs a continuous evaluation to assure uniform and proper application of the acts.

Bureau of International Labor Affairs 

The Bureau was established on December 31, 1959, replacing the Office of International Labor Affairs origi nally established in 1947. Under the policy direction of the Assistant Secretary of Labor for International Affairs, the Bureau is headed by an Administrator who is responsible for discharging Department of Labor functions in the international labor field. Under the policy direction of the Assistant Secretary, the Administrator is also charged with mobilizing, directing, and coordinating all other international activities of the Department's various specialized offices and bureaus. 

These functions and responsibilities of the Bureau include advising on the implications of international labor developments in relation to to U.S. foreign and domestic policy, analyzing the impact of domestic policy and developments on labor aspects of foreign affairs, recommending operations designed to promote the United States national interest in the foreign labor field generally and with respect to specific areas of the world, and, with the assistance of other offices and bureaus, operating programs affecting labor which are designed to implement foreign policy. 

The Bureau's staff of geographic area specialists develops detailed action programs in the field of labor for the various foreign countries. Through these country programs, the Government's efforts are coordinated to achieve U.S. foreign policy objectives as they relate to labor, abroad. ticipation in the International Labor 

Organization.

Department has membership on the 

Board of the Foreign Service); for representation on delegations and formulation of labor policy in connection with United States participation in the United Nations Economic and Social Council and its various commissions; for participation in the 

Trade Staff Committee and other interagency trade expansion activities. and for staff support for the Department's representatives on the Trade 

Expansion Act Advisory Committee and the Trade Executive Committee; for overseeing the adjustment assistance programs under the Trade Expansion Act; for assisting the Secretary in making determinations for adjustment assistance under the Automotive Products Trade Act of 1965; and for participation of labor missions in the Government's international trade fair program. In these activities the Bureau relies upon technical assistance from other bureaus of the Department.

Bureau of Labor Standards 

 Regulations, Title 

29, Chapter XIII] 

The Bureau, established by departmental order in 1934, is a service agency to State labor departments and officials, and to labor, employer, and civic groups interested in improving working conditions. The Bureau promotes industrial safety and health, develops standards in the field of labor legislation and labor law administration, and carries on programs for international exchange of persons and training. 

LEGISLATIVE AND ADMINISTRATIVE STANDARDS. The Bureau provides technical information and assistance to groups and individuals interested in securing adequate and well administered labor laws. Staff members give technical assistance to State labor departments, management, labor organizations, and civic groups on labor legislation and administration, and in

Bureau of Employees' Compensation 

 Regulations, Title 

20, Chapter I] 

The Bureau, established in 1916, was transferred to the Department of Labor pursuant to Reorganization Plan 19, effective May 24, 1950. The Bureau provides workmen's compensation benefits to injured employees under the following principal acts: 

1. The Federal Employees' Com pensation Act of September 7, 1916, which provides workmen's compensation benefits for civil officers and employees of the United States who suffer personal injuries in the performance of duty. The act has been extended to provide benefits to employees of the District of Columbia Government, excluding the members of its police and fire departments, to temporary members of the Coast Guard Reserve and members of the Coast Guard Auxiliary, the Civil Air Patrol, and the Reserve 

Officers Training Corps; to Peace

Corps volunteers and to Job Corps enrollees and assigned volunteers under the Economic Opportunity Act of 

1964. 

2. The Longshoremen's and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act of March 

4, 1927, which provides workmen's compensation benefits for employees in private enterprise while engaged in maritime employment on navigable waters of the United States. 

3. The District of Columbia Work men's Compensation Act of May 17, 1928, which extends the provisions of the Longshoremen's and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act to private employment in the District of Columbia. 

4. The Defense Base Act of August 

16, 1941, which extends, with certain modifications, the provisions of the Longshoremen's and Harbor Workers' 

Compensation Act to any employment (a) at U.S. military bases outside the continental limits of the United States, (b) under a contract with the United States for the performance of any public work to be performed outside the continental United States, (c) under certain contracts approved and financed by the United States under the Mutual Security Act of 1954, as amended, (d) in the service of the American employers providing welfare or similar services for the benefit of the Armed Forces outside the continental 

United States. 

5. The War Hazards Compensation 

Act of December 2, 1942, which provides benefits for persons engaged in the employments listed under the Defense Base Act who suffer injury or death as a result of a war risk hazard, payments to dependents of employees missing from the place of employment due to the belligerent action of a hostile force, and reimbursement to an employer or insurance ployer or insurance company for payment made under the Defense Base Act on account of an injury caused by war hazard. 

6. Provisions of the Outer Conti nental Shelf Lands Act of August 7, 1953, extending the Longshoremen's and Harbor Workers' Compensation

Act to operations conducted on the 

Outer Continental Shelf. 

7. The Nonappropriated Fund In strumentalities Act of July 18, 1958, extending the Longshoremen's and Harbor Workers' Act to employees of nonappropriated fund instrumentalities of the Armed Forces, such as Army and Air Force Exchange Service.
