Employees' Compensation Appeals 

Board [For regulations codified under this head ing, see Code of Federal Regulations, Title 20, Chapter IV] The Employees' Compensation Ap peals Board was established in the Federal Security Agency by Reorganization Plan 2, effective July 16, 1946. Reorganization Plan 19, effective May 24, 1950, provided for the transfer of the Board and its functions to the Department of Labor.

The Board consists of three members appointed by the Secretary of Labor, one of whom is designated as chairman and administrative officer. The function of the Board is to consider and decide appeals from final decisions of the Director, Bureau of Employees' 

Compensation, and of the Governor of the Canal Zone in cases arising under the Federal Employees' Compensation

Act (5 U.S.C. 8101). (For coverage of The Commissioner of Labor Statis tics has responsibility for the Department's labor statistics activities. He supervises the Bureau of Labor

Statistics. 

the Federal Employees' Compensation 

Act, see Bureau of Employees' Compensation.) Appeals may be taken to the Board on disputed questions of law and facts, and on the basis of abuse or failure to exercise discretion.

Commissioner of Labor Statistics Bureau of Labor Statistics 

The Bureau of Labor, the predecessor of the Bureau of Labor Statistics, was established in the Department of the Interior, by act of June 27, 1884.

In 1913, after several changes in status, it became the Bureau of Labor Statistics in the newly created Department of Labor. The Bureau is the Govern ment's principal factfinding agency in the field of labor economics, particularly with respect to the collection and analysis of data on employment and manpower, productivity and technological developments, wages, industrial relations, work injuries, prices, and costs and standards of living.

An appeal may be filed pursuant to the Board's rules of procedure which may be found in title 20 of the Code of Federal Regulations, Part 501. Application for review forms may be obtained from the Board, but informal applications which set forth grounds of the appeal are also acceptable. 

New evidence may not be submitted to the Board; its review is limited to the evidence in the case record. The appeals procedure includes, upon request, a hearing for the presentation of oral argument. In cases reviewed upon the merits, the decision contains a written opinion setting forth the reasons for action taken. The decisions of the 

Board are final. The Bureau has no enforcement or administrative functions. Practically all of the basic data it collects from workers, businessmen, and from other governmental agencies are supplied by voluntary cooperation based on their interest in and need for the analyses and summaries which result. The research and statistical projects planned by the Bureau grow out of the needs of these groups, as well as the needs of Congress and the Federal and State governments. The information collected is issued in special bulletins and in its official publication, the Monthly 

Labor Review.

EMPLOYMENT AND THE LABOR 

FORCE. Data are published each month on the labor force, employment, and unemployment, by age, sex, occupation, etc., based on a sample survey of the population. At recurring intervals the surveys provide estimates

of the educational attainment of the labor force, the employment of students, family relationship of workers, and other personal and economic characteristics of the labor force. 

National estimates are published each month on the employment of wage and salary workers in 401 manufacturing and nonmanufacturing industries. National labor turnover rates are provided for 224 industries in manufacturing, mining, and communications. In cooperation with State agencies, comparable employment and labor turnover data are provided for all of the States and for larger metropolitan areas. Comprehensive analyses, together with all the Government's current statistics on labor force, employment, and unemployment are published monthly in Employment and

Earnings and Monthly Report on the 

Labor Force. 

The Bureau conducts studies of trends in unemployment, of problems affecting particular groups in the working population, such as youth and older workers, and prepares analyses and projections of the changing size and composition of the labor force. In addition, the Bureau is responsible for assessment of the military manpower pool and for projections of potential manpower resources, in relation to requirements under conditions of national emergency.

Exploratory research is now being undertaken looking toward the development of a system of statistics on job vacancies. Such data will contribute greatly to the improvement of knowledge about various job markets and will be useful in interpreting trends in the levels of unemployment and the requirements for manpower development and retraining.

AVERAGE HOURS AND EARNINGS.- 

Gross average hourly and weekly earnings, and average weekly hours, for production or nonsupervisory workers, are issued currently by the Bureau for about 352 industries on a national 234-298-67-23 basis. Average weekly overtime hours are published currently for 146 manufacturing industry groups. Through the cooperative State program, similar data are made available for all States and the more important metropolitan areas. These statistics are reported monthly in Employment and Earnings and Monthly Report on the Labor Force.

OCCUPATIONAL STATISTICS AND ANAL- 

YSIS. Reports are published on the long-range employment outlook in important occupations and industries. 

Data on employment trends, earnings, hours, industrial hazards, collective bargaining agreements, and technological trends collected by the Bureau are included for guidance purposes, together with information from other Government and private sources. Conclusions of these studies are published in the Occupational Outlook Quarterly, a periodical issued four times in the school year, and biennially in the 

Occupational Outlook Handbook. 

Plans are now being implemented to obtain current employment statistics by occupation, with the goal of developing a regular annual statistical series on employment in about 100 of the skilled, and clerical occupations. Such most important professional, technical, data are needed to refine estimates of future occupational requirements and opportunities, to evaluate the impact of automation and technological change and shift in demand on the occupational structure of the labor force, and to measure the effectiveness of training and education programs in meeting needs for skilled workers. 

WAGES AND INDUSTRIAL RELA- 

TIONS.-Occupational wage surveys are made annually in 85 major labor areas. These studies provide information on the level and distribution of wages and salaries for office clerical, professional and technical, maintenance and power plant, and custodial, warehousing, and shipping occupational categories. Work schedules and

supplementary wage benefits are also summarized in these studies. More limited occupational wage surveys are made in many additional areas to provide data for the administration of the 

McNamara-O'Hara Service Contract 

Act. A more comprehensive national survey of salaries for professional, administrative, technical, and clerical occupations is made annually. 

Occupational wage surveys are made in selected industries covering major manufacturing and nonmanufacturing industries over a 5-year cycle. A few industries are studied annually; most industries, however, are studied at 3to 5-year intervals. Information is provided on a national and regional basis and for selected areas of concentration. Work schedules and supplementary wage benefits are also summarized in these studies. Annual surveys are made in 68 cities of wage rates agreed upon in union contracts for a limited number of occupations in printing and publishing, local streetcar and bus operations, the building trades, and motor trucking. Quarterly data are available for 100 cities for seven selected occupations in the construction trades.

Distributions of production and related workers and of other nonsupervisory employees by straight-time average hourly earnings are periodically established in studies that provide national and regional estimates for manufacturing and selected nonmanufacturing industries for minimum wage legislation and other purposes.

Information on current trends in wage rates and wage practices is presented in a monthly report summarizing current wage settlements. In addition, statistical summaries are prepared quarterly and annually. Chronologies showing the historical development of wage rate changes are presented for important bargaining situations in selected industries. A series of indexes of changes in wages and salaries for selected occupational groups are maintained. 

Studies of employer expenditures on compensation and its structure and the composition of payroll hours are made over a 2-year cycle in the total private nonagriculture sector and in selected manufacturing and nonmanufacturing industries.

The Bureau maintains a file of current union contracts and constitutions which is used as factual background material by unions, employers, and conciliation agencies in the settlement of industrial disputes, and as a guide to the preparation of new agreements. 

The Bureau publishes analyses of union agreement provisions concerning such subjects as arbitration and griev ances, job security issues, wage provisions, and paid leave provisions. Similar studies of health, insurance, and pension plans, and other employee benefit plans and of the substantive provisions of union constitutions are also made. Current statistics on work disputes are issued monthly with destoppages resulting from industrial tailed analyses available annually. The 

Bureau publishes a biennial Directory of National and International Labor

Unions in the United States, and studies of union membership, structure, and procedures. At irregular intervals it conducts a membership survey of single employer and unaffiliated local unions. 

PRODUCTIVITY MEASUREMENT.-The 

Bureau publishes annual indexes of output per man-hour and unit manhour requirements for the private economy and broad economic sectors such as agriculture, manufacturing, and nonmanufacturing. Annual indexes are published comparing trends in productivity with those of employment costs per hour, employment costs per unit of output, and prices for the total private nonagricultural and manufacturing sectors of the economy. Indexes are also prepared for selected industries in manufacturing and nonmanu-

JAZA  

347 facturing relating output to the manhours of production workers and of all employees. 

STUDIES IN TECHNOLOGY.-The 

Bureau conducts studies of technological developments and automation and their implications for productivity and manpower requirements. These studies explore the technological outlook among industries and the impact of major innovations across industry lines. 

These studies also deal with the adjustments made by plants introducing new kinds of equipment, including planning, training, and transfer of workers, the outlook for innovations and for technological developments in different industries, with the projected impact on productivity and changes in number and kind of workers who will be needed.

LABOR REQUIREMENTS. Studies of the importance of construction in generating employment include estimates for direct, on-site construction activities and for indirect, off-site activities such as manufacturing, mining, and transportation. They also provide information on the kind of construction labor used, the timing of construction, and the kinds of materials used. 

ECONOMIC GROWTH.-The Bureau performs research and coordinating functions in relation to the program of work on economic growth and employment opportunities, utilizing a wide range of data including the effects of trends in population, labor force, employment, productivity, interindustry relationship, pattern of consumer expenditures investment, Government expenditures, foreign trade, etc., on various economic models and projections. high accident rates, to determine accident causes and thereby to stimulate accident prevention programs in the industries studied. 

INDUSTRIAL SAFETY.-The Bureau conducts surveys on work injuries in both manufacturing and nonmanufacturing industries. National estimates are prepared annually for all disabling work injuries, by extent of disability for major industry groups. Special studies are made in industries with Technical services are extended to State agencies to assist them in the development of better accident statistics. Currently, State-Federal cooperative injury rate surveys are conducted in 13 States.

PRICES AND LIVING CONDITIONS.- 

The Bureau is the principal agency of the Federal Government concerned with price statistics outside the field of agriculture. It is also responsible for conducting surveys of family expenditures and incomes, developing family budget studies, and analyzing changes in levels and standards of living. 

The Bureau computes a Consumer Price Index for the Nation which is published monthly. Retail prices are collected regularly in 56 cities for food and for other items such as clothing, house furnishings, miscellaneous goods and services, and rents. In addition to a U.S. index, city indexes are published monthly for the 5 largest cities and quarterly for 18 other cities.

The Wholesale Price Index includes primary market prices of over 2,300 raw materials, semimanufactured goods, and manufactured goods, divided into 15 major groups, 85 subgroups, 288 product classes. These data are also classified into 34 indexes by stage of processing, 8 indexes by durability of product, and 23 other special purpose indexes. The Bureau maintains records of price quotations for over 7,000 series for goods sold in primary markets. Primary market price indexes are published monthly. Price indexes for over 60 industries are also published, classified according to the 

Standard Industrial Classification. In addition, the Bureau publishes a daily index of spot market prices. 

Studies of consumer expenditures and income are conducted from time to time. Such studies were made in 66 cities during 1961 and 1962, and in 5

Services concerned with real property, space, communications, messenger service, central mail room facilities, parking space facilities, travel arrange-

ments, local transportation facilities, procurement of articles and services, centralized duplicating and printing, and centralized stock and shipping rooms are provided by the Office on a departmentwide basis. Preparation of the budget for the Office of the Secretary and certain bureaus and offices and the provision of centralized accounting and payroll services are also responsibilities of the Office. 

Responsibility for the development and coordination of all plans and procedures necessary to provide management, fiscal, and administrative services for the execution of the mobilization and civil defense responsibility of the Department, including communications, establishing and maintaining relocation sites, safeguarding records and providing physical security measures, rests with the Office. 

The Office directs and coordinates the personnel program of the Department and is responsible for the standards, procedures, and methods under which the program operates. It also directs management programs to improve employee-management relations, employee morale, employee training and utilization, and employee work performance appraisal and improvement. 

LIBRARY.-The Library is a special ized collection of over 400,000 books, periodicals, and pamphlets on labor and related subjects. It provides reference service to the staff of the Department and to the public, circulates books and periodicals to the staff, and lends material to other libraries. Approved.

Welfare was created by Reorganization 

Plan 1 of 1953. Under provisions of the act approved April 1, 1953 (67 

Stat. 18; 5 U. S. C. 623), the Plan became effective on April 11, 1953. The

Plan abolished the Federal Security 

Agency, created by Reorganization Plan I of 1939, and transferred all functions of the Federal Security Ad ministrator to the Secretary of Health,

SECRETARY.-The Secretary of

PURPOSE.—The Department was established for the purpose of improving the administration of those agencies of the Government the major responsibilities of which are to promote the general welfare in the fields. of health, education, and social security.

ORGANIZATION.—The Department is administered under the supervision and direction of the Secretary. House for the Blind, Gallaudet College, Howard University. He represents the Secretary in the development of

CREATION AND AUTHORITY.— -The Public Health Service has its origin in an act of July 16, 1798 (ch. 77, 1 Stat. 

605), authorizing marine hospitals for the care of American merchant seamen. Subsequent legislation has vastly broadened the scope of its activities. 

The Public Health Service Act of 

July 1, 1944 (58 Stat. 682; 42 U. S. C. 

201), consolidated and revised substantially all existing legislation relat ing to the Public Health Service. The basic Public Health Service legal re sponsibilities have been broadened and expanded many times since 1944. 

Major organizational transfers have included vital statistics activities (1946), health services for the American Indians (1955), and the National 

Library of Medicine (1956).

Other important functions added include grants for the construction of hospitals and medical facilities and for health research facilities, expanded grants to States for health services, John F. Kennedy Federal

ticularly with reference to public and intergovernmental relations. The De partment maintains nine regional offices. financial assistance to health professions educational institutions, national health survey responsibilities, expanded programs for air pollution control and solid waste disposal, grants for the establishment of community mental health centers and for facilities for the mentally retarded, grants for the establishment of regional medical programs, and grants to State and local agencies for comprehensive health planning. 

PURPOSE.-The Public Health Serv ice, under the direction of the Surgeon

General, is the Federal agency specifically charged with responsibilities for protecting and improving the health of the people of the Nation. It is also responsible for collaborating with governments of other countries and with international organizations in world health activities. The major functions of the Service are: (1) to conduct and support research and research training in the medical and related sciences including health services and the dis-

semination of medical knowledge, (2) to conduct and support research, training, and service programs in the area of mental health, (3) to increase the supply and improve the qualifications of health manpower, (4) to provide medical and hospital services to persons authorized to receive care from the Service and to aid in the development of community health services including hospitals and related facilities, and (5) to prevent the introduction of communicable diseases into the United States and to promote the application of new knowledge for the prevention and control of disease and the maintenance of a healthy environment. 

ORGANIZATION.-Presidential Reorganization Plan 3 of 1966 authorized a complete reorganization of the Public 

Health Service. Under this authority, the Service has been reorganized to consist of: five operating bureaus- 

Bureau of Health Services, Bureau of

Health Manpower, Bureau of Disease Prevention and Environmental Con trol, National Institutes of Health, and a National Institute of Mental Health; two major activities reporting directly to the Surgeon General-the National 

Library of Medicine and the National 

Center for Health Statistics; and an

Office of the Surgeon General. 

The National Advisory Health 

Council and the advisory councils established for each major program area provide overall advice and policy guidance to the Surgeon General and review all research grant applications in their area of competence. Advice and consultation is also secured from other advisory groups, from the Board of Regents of the National Library of 

Medicine, and from the Conference of

State and Territorial Health Officers. 

of Health, Education, and Welfare. 

These staffs are headed by regional health directors who represent the Surgeon General in interpreting and carrying out the broad policies of the Service. The regional staffs work with 

State authorities in developing and maintaining plans, programs, and budgets for Federal-State cooperative health programs. In order to maintain direct contact with State and local authorities, with field offices of other Federal agencies, and with other official and nonofficial organizations concerned with its activities, the Service maintains a staff in the regional offices of the Department 

Office of the Surgeon General The Office of the Surgeon General provides staff assistance to the Surgeon General in managing and directing the activities of the Service. Its various divisions and offices are involved in: (1) determining national health needs. and planning and evaluating programs to meet these needs; (2) coordinating grant and contract policies; (3) planning and coordinating international health activities; (4) administering comprehensive health planning and development grant programs; (5) directing and coordinating information, publications, and public inquiries activities; (6) developing personnel policies and coordinating personnel management programs; (7) developing policy and coordinating operations in overall management activities such as finance, procurement, and facility planning; (8) assuring that health facilities and programs which receive Federal support are conducted on a nondiscriminatory basis; and (9) directing the 

Public Health Service regional orga nization.

NATIONAL CENTER FOR HEALTH STATISTICS.-The Center serves as the principal statistical arm of the Public Health Service and one of the major general purpose statistical organizations of the Government. This organization conducts continuing surveys and special studies of the Nation's population to determine the extent of illness and disability, to gather information related to these conditions, and to serve as a basis for predicting health trends. It collects and dissemi-

1 14 41 4a 24. • nates data on national health resources, including facilities and manpower. 

It also cooperates with the States in the collection of vital statistics (births, deaths, marriages, and divorces) and is the only source of national tabulation and analysis of such data. The Center also sponsors cooperative studies in foreign countries which provide useful comparative statistical data. 

NATIONAL LIBRARY OF MEDICINE.- The National Library of Medicine as sists the advancement of medicine and related sciences through the collection, dissemination, and exchange of the world's biomedical literature. Holdings of the Library comprise the greatest collection of medical literature in the world. Bibliographic access to its collections is provided through 

MEDLARS, a computerized informa tion storage and retrieval system, and through the publication of guides in the form of catalogs, indexes, and bib liographies. Physical access to to the literature is provided through interlibrary loans, photoduplication, and reference services.

The Library serves as a national medical information resource for medical education, research and service activities of Federal and private agencies, organizations, institutions, and individuals. It supports the translation and publication of biomedical literature. It provides support for medical library development and for training of biomedical librarians and other health information specialists. It conducts and supports research in techniques and methods for recording, storing, retrieving, and communicat ing health information. The Library also provides technical consultation services and research assistance. 

Bureau of Disease Prevention and Environmental Control The Bureau of Disease Prevention and Environmental Control encom passes those Public Health Service programs designed to prevent or control communicable and other diseases, chronic illness and disability, accidental injuries, health hazards from air pollution, radiation, and other forms. of environmental contamination. It maintains surveillance of illness and deaths associated with specific diseases and conditions, monitors contaminants in the environment which may be harmful to health and studies their relationships to morbidity and mortality, establishes human tolerance levels for environmental contaminants, and studies social and economic influences of urbanization and industrial development on environmental health.

It conducts, supports, and evaluates research and demonstrations directed toward improved methods for preventing and controlling disease, accidental injury, and environmental hazards; supports and provides technical advice on national and international disease eradication programs; provides technical assistance to health authorities on epidemiological investigations and laboratory services; and administers interstate and foreign quarantine regulations.

Bureau of Health Manpower The Bureau of Health Manpower serves as the Public Health Service fo cal point for developing and coordi nating programs designed to provide additional, better qualified, and more effectively utilized personnel for the 

Nation's health services.

It develops, conducts, and supports programs to assess current and future health manpower requirements, increase the supply and availability, improve the quality and utilization, and evaluate the effectiveness of health manpower as well as education and training programs and facilities for the health occupations; develops and implements PHS manpower policies; designs legislative proposals for needed health manpower programs and initiates the implementation of such pro-

grams; promotes activities to stimulate interest in health careers; coordinates

PHS manpower programs (supplyrequirements, utilization, and secondary, collegiate, graduate, continuing, and speciality education) and maintains requisite relationships for the 

Service with Federal and non-Federal organizations; provides leadership and technical assistance in planning, initiating, conducting, coordinating, and evaluating the Nation's health manpower programs; and serves as a national clearinghouse for information on health manpower needs, resources, utilization, and education and training programs. 

Bureau of Health Services The Bureau of Health Services is a central resource for improving the quality and accessibility of health care for the American people. It combines the direct medical care responsibi ties of the Public Health Service with responsibilities for supporting the planning and construction of health facilities, the development of new systems for providing community personal health services, and the establishment of quality standards for all health services. 

The Bureau provides health and dental care to eligible beneficiaries through a system of Public Health 

Service hospitals and outpatient clinics. It provides medical care and preventive public health services to Indians and Alaska natives. It administers health care programs for the Bu reau of Prisons, U.S. Coast Guard, Bu reau of Employees' Compensation, and the Peace Corps, and provides technical advice and personnel to assist other 

Federal agencies in developing health care programs for their employees or beneficiaries. The Bureau is also responsible for professional direction and staffing of the Surgical Team Project in South Vietnam sponsored by the

Agency for International Develop ment.

The Bureau administers grant programs for the planning and construction of hospitals and related medical facilities, conducts and supports studies leading to the development of new or improved health services systems, develops criteria and standards for health. care and health services, and develops plans for meeting civilian health needs in national emergencies.

National Institutes of Health 

234-298°-67-24 

The National Institutes of Health, the principal research arm of the Public Health Service, is primarily concerned with the extension of basic knowledge regarding the health problems of man and how to cope with them.

It conducts and supports basic and clinical research and research training in the causes, diagnosis, prevention, and cure of diseases of man including the biological effects of environmental contaminants; in the processes of human growth and development; and in related sciences. It conducts laboratory, clinical, and field research; supports health and medically-related research and research training by assisting individuals, universities, institutions, and agencies through grants-in-aid for research projects, training grants, fellowships, grants for the general support of research and research training, and grants for research facilities construction; disseminates and supports dissemination of research findings and related information and supports regional medical cooperative arrangements to apply research results, furnish training, and exchange information among medical schools, research institutions, and hospitals; and through a Division of Biologic Standards administers Federal standards and licensing activities controlling the safety, purity, and potency of certain viruses, serums, toxins, and analagous products sold in interstate commerce.

The statutory functions of the Office of Education are to collect such statistics and facts as shall show the condition and progress of education, to diffuse such information as shall aid the people of the United States in the establishment and maintenance of efficient school systems, and otherwise to promote the cause of edu cation. Subsequent acts and Executive orders have added related functions, including responsibilities for Federal

financial assistance to education and for special studies and programs.

Social Security Administration 

(6401 Security Boulevard, Baltimore, Md., 21235)  Reg ulations, Title 20, Chapter III] 

CREATION AND AUTHORITY.-The Social Security Administration, under a Commissioner for Social Security, was established by the Federal Security Administrator pursuant to Reorgani zation Plan II, effective July 16, 1946, which abolished the Social Security Board (see appendix A) and transferred its functions, along with functions of the Children's Bureau, to the 

Federal Security Administrator. Dele gated to the Commissioner for Social Security were functions in connection with old-age and survivors insurance,

unemployment insurance, public assistance, and most maternal and child welfare programs. Other duties have subsequently been delegated to or transferred from the Administration by law or Presidential order.

The position of Commissioner for Social Security was reestablished as 

Commissioner of Social Security in the 

Department of Health, Education, and

Welfare by Reorganization Plan 1, effective April 11, 1953. The Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare on

January 28, 1963, reorganized the 

Social Security Administration, estab lishing the retirement, survivors, and disability insurance and Federal credit union programs as the primary mis sions of the Administration. The 

Bureau of Old-Age and Survivors

Insurance was abolished as a bureau and the Bureau of Family Services and the Children's Bureau were transferred to a new Welfare Administration.

On July 26, 1965, the Social Security Administration was reorganized to accommodate the new health insurance programs.

PURPOSE. The Social Security Ad ministration administers the Federal retirement, survivors and disability in surance programs (title II of the Social 

Security Act, as amended, and title VII and XI of that act as they pertain to the Social Security Administration), health insurance for the aged programs 

(title XVIII of the Social Security 

Act), and the Federal credit union program (Federal Credit Union Act). 

It is responsible for studying problems of poverty, insecurity, and the health care needs of the aged and the contributions that can be made to their solution by social insurance and related programs and for making recommendations as to the most effective methods of improving social and economic security through social insurance. replacement of earnings lost through old-age or disability retirement or death. These programs provide for the coverage of almost all persons engaged in gainful employment, including the military, the major exceptions being Federal civilian employees under a retirement system; and domestics, agricultural workers, and self-employed persons having very low earnings. Entitlement to benefits is determined from the insured status of the individual; the age and relationship of the individual and his dependents; the application for such benefits; and in the case of disability benefits, the extent and expected duration of disability. Benefits are payable monthly in amounts related to the average monthly earnings of the insured person. A lump sum death benefit is payable under certain conditions. 

The purpose of retirement, survivors, and disability insurance programs is to provide continuing income for individuals and their families as partial The health insurance program (hospital and supplementary medical insurance) provides the aged with basic protection against the costs of hospital care, and physicians' services, and certain other health and medical services. All social security and railroad retirement beneficiaries are entitled to hospital insurance benefits when they attain age 65. (For an interim period most persons who are age 

65, or will attain age 65 in the near future, but who are not eligible for social security or railroad retirement benefits are also entitled to protection under hospital insurance.) Persons who have attained age 65 are eligible to enroll for the supplementary medical insurance, sharing the premium payment with the Government. 

The Federal credit union program promotes thrift by encouraging cooperative, systematic saving and by making credit available in the short-term, small loan field at reasonable rates of interest, for credit union members. To accomplish these purposes, Federal credit unions provide convenient facilities for encouraging the development of habits of consistent, regular saving out of current earnings.

HEADQUARTERS ORGANIZATION.-The Social Security Administration, with headquarters offices in Baltimore, Md., is composed of the Office of the Commissioner, five staff offices, and seven operating bureaus, as described below. 

The Office of the Commissioner includes the immediate staff of the Commissioner, Deputy Commissioner, and 

Assistant Commissioner, Field.

The Commissioner of Social Secu rity is responsible for administering the retirement, survivors and disability insurance programs; and for administering the health insurance program with appropriate advice from and consultation with the Public Health Service and the Welfare Administration. This responsibility includes policy determination, program interpretation and evaluation, research oriented to the study of the problems of poverty, insecurity and the health care needs of the aged, and providing recommendations on methods of advancing social and economic security through social insurance. The Commissioner is also responsible for the administration of the Federal Credit Union Act. 

The Deputy Commissioner assists the Commissioner in giving overall executive leadership to the activities of the Social Security Administration and acts for him during his absence or disability.

The Office of the Assistant Commissioner, Field, acts for the Commissioner in coordinating and integrating program administration in the field by giving broad day-to-day direction to the activities of the Regional Assistant Commissioners.

The Office of the Actuary prepares long- and short-range cost estimates involving such factors as population structure and mortality, morbidity, wage, employment, and retirement trends in connection with present and proposed social security programs; conducts actuarial studies; and prepares a variety of reports for administrative use and for publication. 

The Office of Administration assists the Commissioner in carrying out the mission of the Social Security Administration, operating in the total area of administration and management of the social security programs, and ini tiating actions to achieve efficient, effective, and economical administration of the programs. The Office helps define the goals of the Social Security Administration; develops and implements management and administrative policies, procedures and systems; assesses performance and initiates action to improve performance in respect to its program, administrative and management objectives; provides advisory and management services to the Commissioner and to the heads of Social 

Security Administration components. 

It represents the Social Security Ad ministration in respect to matters of overall program administration. 

The Office of Information plans and directs a nationwide program of public information to provide public understanding of rights and responsibilities under social security programs. It develops guidelines and techniques applicable to all informational media, and produces a wide range of materials to serve these media; conducts surveys and studies to identify problems and to determine the effectiveness of informational activities; and provides staff direction to SSA's public correspondence activities. 

The Office of Program Evaluation and Planning evaluates the effectiveness of the present SSA program provisions; clarifies and interprets the objectives of the programs; evaluates and develops legislative recommendations; and provides technical and advisory services to congressional committees and individual Congressmen. 

The Office of Research and Statistics plans and conducts long-range research in the general area of human resources and the economic security of the American family; develops extramural cooperative research in social

security under a cooperative research. and demonstration grants program; carries out continuing research in such areas of study as family economics, medical economics, international social security programs and statistics oriented both to meeting SSA program and administration needs and to providing bases for meeting the needs of a wide range of other governmental agencies, research organizations, universities, and scholars. The Office plans, develops, and directs the conduct of large data collection operations related to basic studies of economic and social conditions of the total population. re- The Bureau of Data Processing and Accounts establishes and maintains records of the identity of all holders of Social Security account number cards. 

It receives and records earnings reports data, investigates erroneous reports and earnings discrepancies, and makes necessary adjustments. It also maintains employer identification number records. The Bureau furnishes duplicate account number cards and earnings and status information, upon quest, for title II purposes; certifies earnings record data for claims purposes; and provides statistical data for program and administrative analyses. 

It maintains utilization records for the health insurance program and central EDP beneficiary records. The Bureau operates a large data processing and data transmission facility and provides central EDP systems, programing and machine services. 

The Bureau of Disability Insurance develops and recommends policies relating to the determination of disability under the Social Security 

Act;

evaluates existing policy and develops recommended changes; and issues substantive instructions and interpretive materials to provide basic broad program direction to the disability determination processes and for relating those processes to rehabilitation services.

It coordinates with the 

Bureau of Retirement and Survivors 

Insurance on policies and procedures of mutual concern and application to the retirement, survivors, and disability insurance processes. It formulates management standards and policies for State agencies operating under contractual agreements, and administers a management program to guide, control, and evaluate State agency operations, including the determination of fiscal requirements and allocation of operating funds for each State agency. 

The Bureau reviews State agency disability determinations, authorizes payment or disallowance of benefits in disability cases, maintains disability insurance benefit rolls, and makes disability determinations in cases not covered by State agreements. It represents SSA in disability program coordination and negotiation with other Federal, State, and private organizations, and with the medical profession. It participates in legislative planning, and acts as SSA consultant on disability policy matters. 

The Bureau of District Office 

Operations supervises the operations of approximately 725 social security district and branch offices, which are responsible for: developing public understanding of the purposes and provisions of the retirement, survivors, disability, and health insurance programs and of the public's rights and responsibilities thereunder; assisting the public in filing claims for social security benefits and in enrolling for health insurance; developing and adjudicating claims; conducting investigations relating to earnings records, coverage, and fraud in order to insure accuracy of benefit payments; informing beneficiaries of events which may affect benefit payments, and providing necessary assistance in making appropriate reports; providing effective referral services to other agencies within the community (e.g., rehabilitation, public welfare, legal aid); issuing social security account numbers; TAU TIKKAKY

The Bureau directs the coordination of the health insurance program with all related programs, public and private to (1) assure public knowledge of the programs, (2) stimulate efforts to develop and improve services and facilities, (3) utilize existing knowledge and experience in program operations, and (4) maintain the vitality of the health program in improving the level of health care of the aged population.

The Bureau reviews and approves

State plans for public assistance; reviews State estimates, and certifies to the United States Treasury Federal grants to the States; reviews the operation of State plans for continuing conformity with the Social Security Act; collects, analyzes, and publishes data on the operation of public assistance in the States, including general assistance, and provides technical help to States to improve their programs. 

Public assistance includes financial aid, medical care, and other social services to help recipients achieve their potentialities for self-care, self-support, and strong family life. The extent of financial aid and the provision of services vary between States, reflecting the State's traditions, legislative and administrative structures, community concern, and assistance appropriations. 

The State plan must provide for the program to be in effect in all parts of the State, and for State financial participation. A single State agency must administer the program or supervise its administration. The plan must provide for such methods of administration, including a merit system covering personnel, and for submitting such reports as the Department finds necessary for proper and efficient operation.

The plan must provide for keeping personal information confidential (except as modified by section 618 of the 

Revenue Act of 1951, 65 Stat. 569). 

It cannot set residence and citizenship requirements beyond those named in the Federal law. It must provide for a hearing before the State agency for those who are not satisfied with the action on their cases. In determining need and the amount of the payment, the State must take into account any other income or resources of the person claiming aid. In making these determinations, however, a State must disregard certain amounts and types of income and resources of a blind person and has the option to disregard certain amounts of earned or other income of aged, blind, and disabled individuals and families with dependent children. 

The Social Security Act defines the scope of Federal participation, but does not limit the breadth of State operations. The State may claim Federal money to help needy people living in their own homes, and under certain circumstances, in private institutions, and in public medical institutions. 

The State's payments to assistance recipients for maintenance must be in the form of money. Some medical costs are included in the money payment but most are paid by the agency directly to the medical-care suppliers. 

Under assignment, the Bureau is responsible for assisting the States in developing and maintaining plans for a state of readiness for welfare services in a civil defense emergency, and for continuity and restoration of peacetime welfare programs; performs welfare planning activities in regard to refugees and immigrants, and the repatriation of American nationals from abroad. 

The Economic Opportunity Act of 

1964 (title V) resulted in the Bureau being assigned responsibility for a work experience and training program to help unemployed persons-both those receiving or likely to receive public assistance. 

Children's Bureau [For regulations codified under this head ing, see Code of Federal Regulations, Titl 

42, Chapter II] 

1 The Children's Bureau was create by the act approved April 9, 1912 (3 

Stat. 79, as amended; 42 U, S. C. 19 et seq.) (see also appendix A).

The purpose of the Bureau is to in vestigate and report on all matters re lated to child life and to increase op portunity for the full development o all children by promoting their health and social welfare. It administers title 

V of the Social Security Act. 

The Bureau cooperates with national, State, and local organizations and agencies, both public and voluntary, in planning for the development and extension of services for children and youth.

In carrying out the responsibilities assigned by its organic act, the Bureau makes studies of conditions that are hazards to the well-being of children and of the effectiveness of measures aimed at preventing and alleviating such conditions. On request, it gives advisory service to State and local research and agencies regarding methods of conducting programs aimed at promoting the health and welfare of children. The Bureau provides a clearinghouse of research in child life by collecting and distributing information regarding research studies under way in universities, schools, hos pitals, child research centers, and other public and private agencies throughout the country. 

The Bureau issues both technical and popular publications. Most widely known of its publications for parents is Infant Care. Its Statistical Series presents data on operations of child. health and welfare programs and statistics on the conditions of child life. 

For a representative list of publica tions, see appendix B. 

The Bureau administers, through its- 

Division of Health Services, grants to 

State health agencies for extending and

improving health services for mothers and children. These agencies use the funds to provide health promotion services such as maternity clinics where women get the advice of doctors, nurses, nutritionists, and medical social workers; visits of public health nurses to homes before and after babies are born; well child clinics for child health supervision where mothers can get competent advice on the health care of their babies and preschool children; pediatric clinics; school health programs that spot the youngsters who need medical or dental treatment and help them get it; dental care for children and pregnant women; and immunizations against preventable diseases. Most States conduct special clinics for mentally retarded children where diagnostic, evaluation, counseling, treatment, and followup services are provided. The Bureau provides medical, dental, nursing, nutrition, physical-therapy, and medical-social consultation services to State health agencies administering such services. 

Through its Division of Health Serv ices, the Bureau administers a 5-year program of grants to provide maternity and infant care. State health agencies or, with the consent of such agencies, the health agencies of any political subdivisions of the States use these grants to provide medical care to women who during the maternity period are unlikely to receive necessary health care because they are from families with low incomes or for other reasons. In addition to medical care for the mother, health care for mothers and infants following childbirth is included. The health care is available particularly to prospective mothers who have or are likely to have conditions associated with childbearing which increase the hazards to the health of mothers or their infants, including those which may cause physical or mental defects in the infants. to State crippled children's agencies for extending and improving services for crippled children. These agencies, usually in State health or welfare departments, use the funds to locate handicapped children, to provide diagnostic services, and then to see that each child gets the medical care, hospitalization, and continuing care that he needs by a variety of professional people. The 

Bureau provides consultation service to the State agencies on methods and procedures for the early casefinding, the diagnosis, and medical treatment of crippled children and on the development of programs for the care of children with special types of crippling conditions such as epilepsy, poliomyelitis, rheumatic fever, congenital heart disease, and cerebral palsy. The Bureau administers, through its Division of Health Services, grants The Bureau also administers, through its Division of Health Services, special project grants to provide comprehensive health care and services for children of school age, or for preschool children, particularly in areas with concentrations of low-income families. 

Projects provide screening, diagnosis, and preventive services, both medical and dental. Treatment, correction of defects, and aftercare services are provided to children who would not otherwise receive them because of low income or other reasons beyond their control. These grants are available to the State health agency or, with its consent, to the health agency of any political subdivision of the State, to the vising the crippled children's program, State agency administering or superto schools of medicine (with appropriate participation by schools of dentistry) and to teaching hospitals affiliated with schools of medicine.

In fiscal year 1967, the Bureau began to administer a program of grants to institutions of higher learning for training of professional personnel for health and related care of crippled children, particularly mentally retarded children and those with multiple handicaps. 

The professional personnel being trained includes physicians, dentists,

audiologists, nurses, physical therapists, psychologists, and speech and language specialists. 

The Bureau administers, through its Division of Social Services, grants to State public welfare agencies to establish, extend, and strengthen child welfare services. In each State public welfare agency, the division responsible for services to children plans and directs the program for child welfare services. 

Federal funds are used mainly for State staff members to assist in the develop ment of community child welfare programs, for child welfare workers in local communities to provide social services to children, and for training of child welfare staffs. In the administration of these grants the regional staff of the Division of Social Services participates in the development of State plans and gives advisory and consultant service to State public welfare agencies. 

Specialists develop guide materials and provide consultation to national, State, and local public and voluntary agencies in developing services to children in their own homes, foster family care, group care, and institutional care; adoption services; homemaker services; day care services; services to unmarried mothers; and services to mentally retarded children as well. 

Specialists also advise on training of staff in child welfare programs and on State legislation relating to children. 

This division also administers grants for training personnel for work in the field of child welfare by means of funds to institutions of higher learning for curriculum development, traineeships, and short-term training. 

The Bureau administers, through its Division of Research, child welfare research and demonstration grants for projects which are of regional or national significance and for demonstration of new methods or facilities which show promise of substantial contribution to the advancement of child welfare. The Division of Research also administers research grants for studies that may contribute to the advance ment of health services for mothers and children and improve the operation and effectiveness of maternal and child health and crippled children's services. 

The Bureau offers technical assistance in the field of juvenile delinquency to States and communities planning the extension, improvement, and more effective coordination of the various State and local services and facilities required for the treatment and rehabilitation of delinquent youth. 

Consultants are available to advise on the training of personnel for these services; on the content, legislative bases, and administration of juvenile delinquency programs; and on such special types of services as police, juvenile courts, detention, diagnostic and reception centers, training schools, and group work. The Division of Juvenile 

Delinquency Service develops stand ards and guides; makes surveys of services and facilities; cooperates with 

States and localities; and collaborates with voluntary organizations on the development of programs and the training of personnel for services for juvenile delinquents.

Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) 

and serves as the focal point in Government for coordinating the technical advice from appropriate agencies of Government on the programs supported by UNICEF. Vocational Rehabilitation Administration 

Regulations, Title 45, Chapter IV] PURPOSE.-The Vocational Rehabil itation Administration is responsible for the administration of programs to increase the vocational rehabilitation of disabled persons and their greater utilization in gainful and suitable employment. The Administration cooperates with the States and other public and private nonprofit organizations in countries desiring to study maternal and child health and child welfare services for children in the United States. The Children's Bureau is advised in its work by committees and conference groups called to consider special problems. providing these services to the handicapped.

In broad perspective, the overall objective is to provide the leadership and the means for furnishing vocational rehabilitation services promptly and adequately to all the disabled who need and can be expected to benefit from such services.

ACTIVITIES. This agency adminis ters a program of grants to States, which provides a wide range of services to disabled persons, a program of various grants to increase and improve rehabilitation facilities and workshops, and a program licensing blind persons to operate vending stands on Federal or other property. It administers research and training grant programs to improve rehabilitation techniques and to increase the supply of professionally trained rehabilitation personnel. 

1. Support for Services and Facilities. The States have broad authority and responsibility in carrying out their programs of vocational rehabilitation. 

The vocational rehabilitation program may be located under the agency for education or vocational education, in a separate agency concerned primarily with rehabilitation, or in a State agency which includes at least two other organizational units, each of which administers one or more of the major public. education, public health, public welfare, or labor programs of the State. 

In each State which has a separate agency to serve the blind, this agency may function as the sole State agency

MANA? 

responsible for administering that part. of the State plan relating to rehabilitation of the blind.

The vocational rehabilitation program is in effect in the 50 States, the 

District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, the

Virgin Islands, and Guam. There are now 91 State agencies in all, 37 of which serve only the blind.

Strong cooperative relationships are encouraged between State agencies for vocational rehabilitation and all other agencies such as public employment services-which provide services needed in the vocational rehabilitation and job placement processes.

Within the Federal Government, coordinated planning by the Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare and the Secretary of Labor is required to develop and recommend to appropriate State agencies policies and procedures which will promote the employment of disabled men and women who have received services under the rehabilitation program. In addition, the 

Secretaries of these two Departments are directed to work with the Chairman of the President's Committee on 

Employment of the Handicapped in developing methods to secure the maximum use of services of the Committee and its cooperating State and local organizations in promoting employment opportunities for the disabled. 

The Vocational Rehabilitation Ad ministration is responsible for the establishment of standards in the various areas of service; for the approval of 

State plans and amendments; for certification of Federal grants-in-aid to the States and public or other nonprofit organizations and agencies; and for designating the State commission or other agency serving the blind to license blind persons to operate vending stands on Federal or other property. 

It is also responsible, together with the Surgeon General, for approving each application for a project for construction or modernization of a rehabilitation facility under the Hospital and Medical Facilities Amendments of 

1964 (78 Stat. 447; 42 U.S.C. 291c).

The Administration makes a wide variety of grants for the purpose of paying part of the cost of projects for State-wide planning for vocational rehabilitation; State planning to meet rehabilitation facilities needs; construction; and initial staffing of rehabilitation facilities and workshops. The agency also is responsible for workshop improvement grants and activities including a program of technical assistance and, with the advice of a 

National Policy and Performance 

Council, grants to support the provi sion of training services to handicapped individuals in public or other nonprofit workshops and rehabilitation facilities. 

A National Commission on Architectural Barriers to Rehabilitation of the Handicapped has been established to recommend necessary action to achieve full accessibility and use of buildings of all types by the handicapped. Consultation assistance is given the States and other organizations and agencies on a continuing basis by regional assistant commissioners of the Vocational 

Rehabilitation Administration. 

Rehabilitation services include thorough medical diagnosis to determine the extent of disability and possibilities of improvement, to discover possible hidden disabilities, and to determine work capacity; necessary medical, surgical, psychiatric, and hospital treatment; necessary prosthetic devices such as artificial limbs, hearing aids, and braces; individual counseling and guidance; training for jobs; maintenance, training materials, and transportation during rehabilitation, if necessary; occupational tools, equipment, and licenses; placement in the right job; and adjustment services aimed at the mutual satisfaction of worker and employer. The States and Territories purchase rehabilitation services, as required, from existing public or private facilities. Under the 

Federal act, services may be provided without cost to the individual at the

option of a State. For the basic services and the innovation programs, Federal grants authorized and appropriated are matched by State and other public funds, and under certain conditions by funds derived from private sources. FL Men and women with substantial job handicaps in the form of physical or mental impairments can be eligible for services. Three conditions generally must exist before a State rehabilitation agency provides services other than evaluative services: (1) a disability, ce (2) a substantial handicap to employment, and (3) a reasonable expectation that vocational rehabilitation services may render the individual fit to engage in a gainful occupation. If the 

State agency is unable to make a determination promptly with respect to the third condition of eligibility an extended period of evaluation not to exceed 18 months for certain types of disability and 6 months for others may be found acceptable during which services related to the determination may be provided. 0: 121 The disability insurance provisions of the Social Security Act authorize the payment of disability benefits to eligible disabled workers, their dependents, and to the disabled children (beyond age 18) of a retired, deceased, or disabled worker. In all but five 

States, State vocational rehabilitation agencies are responsible, under agreements with the Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare, for preparing the determination of disability benefits. 

All applicants for such benefits must also be referred to the State vocational rehabilitation agency for necessary vocational rehabilitation services to the end that the maximum number of such individuals may be rehabilitated into 1 productive activity. The law provides further that disability benefits may be E withheld for any beneficiary who refuses, without good cause, to accept re- I habilitation services available to him under a State plan approved under the 

Vocational Rehabilitation Act. Under

2. Rehabilitation Research and 

Training. The Vocational Rehabilita tion Administration is responsible for (1) a program of training for personnel and (2) research to advance knowledge of ways of overcoming handicapping conditions. For the training of professional personnel, the Administration conducts a program of training grants to public and voluntary educational institutions and agencies for part of the instructional costs and for scholarship assistance to students. 

Its objectives are: (1) to enlarge the supply of trained personnel for the rehabilitation of physically or mentally handicapped persons; (2) to improve the knowledge and skills of personnel already engaged in rehabilitation services; and (3) to instill a better understanding of rehabilitation philosophy and process on the part of all students enrolled in basic professional training programs preparing personnel for work in rehabilitation services. Rehabilitation research fellowships at the predoctoral and postdoctoral level are awarded to competent research workers in the professional fields which contribute to the vocational rehabilitation of disabled persons. 234-298-67-25 

The Vocational Rehabilitation Ad ministration makes grants to public and other nonprofit organizations and agencies for paying part of the cost of projects for research and demonstrations, research and training centers, and projects for the establishment of special facilities and services which hold promise of making a substantial contribution to the solution of vocational rehabilitation problems common to all or several States. Special project

grants are made upon review and recommendation of a National Advisory 

Council on Vocational Rehabilitation. 

The Administration also is responsible for facilitating utilization of research findings derived from projects supported by funds provided through that administration. as 

3. International Rehabilitation Research and Training. The Vocational Rehabilitation Administration is also responsible for research, research training, the interchange of rehabilitation experts, and other special rehabilitation activities overseas under the Foreign

Currency Program (section 104(k) of the Agricultural Trade Development and Assistance Act of 1954, amended, 72 Stat. 275; 7 U.S.C. 1704, and section 4 of the International 

Health Research Act of 1960, 74 Stat. 

365; 22 U.S.C. 2102). These activities are designed to (1) lead to the development of new knowledge and techniques for eliminating or reducing the handicapping effects of disability or (2) provide new application of existing knowledge and techniques to rehabilitation problems. Research projects are expected to be of mutual benefit to rehabilitation in the United States and in the country in which the project is carried out.

The Vocational Rehabilitation Ad ministration also plans and develops training programs in rehabilitation suited to the needs of nationals of other countries. These activities are carried out in cooperation with the United Nations and its specialized agencies, the Agency for International 

Development, the Department of

State, and numerous voluntary organizations.

Regulations, Title 45, Chapter IX] PURPOSE.- -The Administration on 

Aging provides a strong central focus for the Federal Government's concern for the needs and problems of the aging population, and national leadership in meeting these needs and solving these problems.

OFFICE OF ADMINISTRATION. -The 

Office conducts the administrative, financial, and personnel management activities of the Administration; manages the financial aspects of grants and contracts administration; performs management appraisal of program operations; and provides advice to State agencies and project grantees on management problems.

OFFICE OF PROGRAM POLICY AND IN- FORMATION. The Office analyzes and evaluates the impact of existing programs of the Administration on Aging and other agencies on the problems

and needs of the aging; identifies needed improvements in program coordination, program content or coverage, or changes in program goals; develops proposals for such improvements in Administration programs; suggests improvements to other agencies whose programs affect the aging; and develops liaison with these agencies to stimulate program coordination and mutual support. It provides secretariat services for the Advisory Committee on Older Americans and the President's Council on Aging. 

It also serves as a clearinghouse for information related to problems of the aged and aging, and information as to services and opportunities available; identifies gaps in coverage of these areas and takes action to meet the need or stimulate other sources to meet the need; prepares and publishes periodicals on aging programs and services; and prepares and disseminates educational materials directed primarily at professional aging specialists or the aging population.

OFFICE OF STATE AND COMMUNITY SERVICES.—This Office plans and carries out a program of Federal grants to States for community planning and coordination of programs for the aging, establishment of new or expansion of existing programs such as multipurpose senior centers, demonstrations, and training under title III of the Older Americans Act; develops policies, standards, and guides; provides consultation and technical assistance to the States and their political subdivisions on development of priorities, program development, and operation; reviews and approves State plans; evaluates the administration of State plans and advises on improvements; and stimulates State and local program innovation and progress in the extension of services and opportunities for the aging and the intermeshing of programs. It also plans and carries out for the Office of Economic Opportunity the stimulation, development, and supervision of locally initiated demonstration projects for the employment of the elderly poor; develops models of desirable projects (e.g., Foster Grandparent Program); provides consultation on project development; evaluates project proposals and recommends funding by OEO; evaluates project progress and recommends program and budget changes; evaluates project results in terms of the desirability of continued support and use of findings in the development of model projects; recommends on continuation of projects to OEO. 

OFFICE OF RESEARCH, DEMONSTRA- TIONS, AND TRAINING.-The Office analyzes existing knowledge of problems and needs of the aging; identifies gaps in this knowledge and plans to develop needed knowledge through the functions of the Administration on Aging or other programs. It plans and carries out programs of Federal grants to, and contracts with, public and nonprofit private agencies, organizations, and institutions for research, development, demonstration, and training projects, and contracts with individuals for research, development, and demonstration projects, under titles IV and V of the Older Americans Act; develops policies, requirements, and guides; stimulates the development of innovative projects in underdeveloped areas of the broad field of aging; provides consultative services to prospective applicants; provides secretariat services for the advisory committees on research and demonstrations and training; evaluates project proposals; awards grants and contracts; and evaluates project progress and results in terms of the desirability of continued support and use of findings. It also gathers and analyzes statistics in the field of aging; identifies levels of activity, trends, and problems; and conducts research and training in selected areas to supplement the program of grants and contracts.

CREATION AND AUTHORITY.--The Department of Housing and Urban 

Development was established by the 

Department of Housing and Urban Development Act of September 9, 1965 

(79 Stat. 667; 5 U.S.C. 642). The act, which became effective November 9, 1965, transferred to and vested in the 

Secretary of Housing and Urban De velopment all of the functions, powers, and duties of the Housing and Home Finance Agency (including the Community Facilities Administration and the Urban Renewal Administration), of the Federal Housing Administration and the Public Housing Administra tion, and of the heads and other officers and offices of those agencies. The act also transferred to the Department the 

Federal National Mortgage Associa tion.

of national purpose, sound development of the Nation's communities and metropolitan areas in which the vast majority of its people live and work. "To carry out such purpose, and in recognition of the increasing importance of housing and urban development in our national life, the Congress finds that establishment of an executive department is desirable to achieve the best administration of the principal programs of the Federal Government which provide assistance for housing and for the development of the Nation's communities; to assist the 

President in achieving maximum coordination of the various Federal activities which have a major effect upon urban community, suburban, or metropolitan development; to encourage the solution of problems of housing, urban development, and mass transportation through State, county, town, village, or other local and private action, including promotion of interstate, regional, and metropolitan cooperation; to encourage the maximum

contributions that may be made by vigorous private homebuilding and mortgage lending industries to housing, urban development, and the national economy; and to provide for full and appropriate consideration, at the national level, of the needs and interests of the Nation's communities and of the people who live and work in them."

Federal Housing Administration The Federal Housing Administra tion carries out the following programs of the Department:

Programs of loan and mortgage insurance authorized by the National Housing Act, intended for the following purposes: 

PROPERTY IMPROVEMENT LOAN IN- SURANCE. Title I, section 2, provides co-insurance on loans primarily for alterations, repairs, or improvements; section 203 (k) provides mortgage insurance on home improvements; and section 220 (h) authorizes mortgage insurance on improvements in approved urban renewal or disaster areas. 

HOME MORTGAGE INSURANCE. -Sec tion 203, the primary program of the act, provides mortgage insurance on one- to four-family housing. Special considerations are authorized for military veterans. Section 203(h) provides more liberal terms for disaster housing and section 203 (i) authorizes special considerations for housing in nonurban areas. Section 222 provides special mortgage insurance for servicemen on active duty.

RENTAL HOUSING.-Section 207 pro vides mortgage insurance on rental housing of eight or more units and on mobile-home courts.

COOPERATIVE HOUSING.-Section 

213 authorizes mortgage insurance on cooperative housing of five or more units as well as supplementary loans for improvement or repair or resale of memberships.

URBAN RENEWAL HOUSING.-Section 

220 provides mortgage insurance on single-family or multifamily housing in approved urban renewal areas. 

LOW- OR MODERATE-INCOME HOUS- 

ING.-Section 221 authorizes mortgage insurance on single-family or multifamily housing, primarily for families. from urban renewal areas. Section 

221(d)(3) authorizes below-market interest rates for rental housing where special low rents are offered.

Section 221 (h) authorizes mortgage insurance for the purchase and rehabilitation of substandard or deteriorated housing by nonprofit organizations for resale to low-income purchasers. 

HOUSING FOR THE ELDERLY.-Sec tion 231 provides mortgage insurance on rental housing for elderly or handicapped persons.

NURSING HOMES.-Section 232 au thorizes mortgage insurance on rental properties designed to provide nursing home facilities.

EXPERIMENTAL HOUSING.-Section 

233 provides mortgage insurance on single-family or multifamily housing with experimental design or materials.

CONDOMINIUM HOUSING.-Section 

234 provides mortgage insurance on individually owned units in multifamily projects.

YIELD INSURANCE.-Title VII in sures investment returns on multifamily housing. 

ARMED SERVICES HOUSING. Title 

VIII provides mortgage insurance on single-family or multifamily housing for sale or rent primarily to military or civilian personnel of the armed serv ices, National Aeronautics and Space Administration, or Atomic Energy 

Commission. 

LAND DEVELOPMENT.---Title X pro vides mortgage insurance on property purchased for the development of building sites.

GROUP MEDICAL PRACTICE FACILI- TIES. Title XI authorizes mortgage insurance for the financing of construction and equipment of facilities for the group practice of medicine, optometry, or dentistry. 

The rent supplement program authorized by section 101 of the Housing and Urban Development Act of 1965 

(79 Stat. 451; 12 U.S.C. 1701s), which provides for the payment of rent supplements to approved multifamilyhousing owners under section 221(d) (3) (market interest rate) and experimentally, under sections 221(d)(3) (below market interest rate) and 231.

Disposition (including management

and liquidation of Government-owned mortgages) of Government-owned property at Richland, Wash.; Los 

Alamos, N. Mex.; and Oak Ridge,

Tenn., under the Atomic Energy Community Act of 1955, as amended and 

Executive Orders 10657 and 11105.

Office of Intergovernmental Rela tions and Urban Program Coordination

The Office, headed by a Director, conducts studies and analyses and provides staff assistance to the Assistant 

Secretary and Deputy Assistant Secretary in matters of intergovernmental relations and urban program coordination, including representing the Department in the development of effective working relationships with other Federal agencies that have a

major impact on community development; providing a source of information and advice with respect to problems arising in the administration of Federal programs requiring effective cooperation among the Federal, State, and local governmental units and agencies concerned; assisting and encouraging State, county, and local governments in the development of intergovernmental arrangements that will assist them in the more effective discharge of their responsibilities for program administration; and consulting with State, local, and regional officials and securing their recommendations with respect to these matters.

Office of Urban Studies and 

Clearinghouse Services

The Office, headed by a Director, administers the following programs and activities: 

Housing research and urban studies authorized by the Housing Acts of 1948, 1956, and 1957, as amended; grants to assist and demonstrate slum clearance and urban renewal methods and techniques under section 314 of the Housing Act of 1954, as amended; and grants to develop and demonstrate new or improved means of providing housing for low-income and handicapped persons and families under section 207 of the Housing Act of 1961, as amended.

The provisions of technical assistance, studies, and publications relating to open-space land and urban beautification and improvement, under section 708 of the Housing Act of 1961, as amended.

The conduct of studies, research, and demonstration projects for the development and improvement of techniques and methods for comprehensive planning and for the advancement of the purposes of the Urban Planning Grant Program, as authorized under section 701(b) of the Housing Act of 1954, as amended.

The conduct of the study of housing and building codes, zoning, tax policies, and development standards authorized in section 301 of the Housing and 

Urban Development Act of 1965. 

The establishment and provision of technical advisory services to assist municipalities and other political subdivisions in the budgeting, financing, planning, and construction of community facilities, under section 207 of the 

Housing Amendments of 1955, as amended.

The conduct of surveys of the status and current volume of State and local public works planning and surveys of estimated requirements for State and local public works, under section 702 (f) of the Housing Act of 1954, as amended.

The study of alternative programs for providing financial assistance in connection with natural disasters, under the Southeast Hurricane Dis aster Relief Act of 1965. 

The development and administration of a clearinghouse service to supply information covering the activities mentioned above and all aspects of housing and urban development for the benefit of States, counties, and urban areas. 

The Office also exercises supervision over the conduct of comprehensive market analyses to serve Department programs.
